title: tron: Rebuild moe_routing in place across forward passes
author: bgamari-positron
body:
Each MoE routing step currently constructs a fresh `moe_routing`, discarding the previous object's vector storage even when successive steps use the same state field. This change rebuilds that object in place so its routing buffers retain capacity across routing steps and forward passes.

## Rebuild the routing without replacing its storage

Model state now holds a `moe_routing<N, K>` directly instead of an optional that is replaced on each build. Both routing builders fill a caller-owned object through an output parameter. Generated C++ and the handwritten MoE implementation adopt this API, including the handwritten forced-routing path.

Illustrative pseudocode for generated routing:

```cpp
// Before: construct a new object and replace the previous one.
routing.emplace(build_moe_routing_from_indices(...));

// After: rebuild the existing object, retaining its buffers.
build_moe_routing_from_indices(..., routing);
```

`moe_routing::reset` clears and refills the per-expert row lists, the flat expert-ordered token/slot list, and the token-to-batch-rank map while preserving their allocated capacity. Later builds reuse those allocations when their sizes fit; larger batches or more imbalanced expert assignments can still grow the buffers.

The routing holds a rebindable pointer to the caller-owned per-token selections, allowing default construction followed by an in-place build. Those selections must remain alive through subsequent routing use. Reset also recomputes the active experts and invalidates every old batch rank before assigning current ranks, preventing tokens absent from the new batch from retaining a stale rank. Expert views, schedules, and routing statistics consume the persistent object directly.

The existing routing channel continues to publish the routing only after worker 0 has finished rebuilding it and constructing its expert-matmul schedules, so helper workers cannot consume partially rebuilt state.

## Stack scope

The parent, [#4461](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4461), makes compatible routings with sufficiently separated lifetimes share a state field while preserving their logical router identities. This layer lets the object in that field retain its internal vector capacity across uses. Routing ownership, compatibility checks, and logical router identity come from the preceding stack layers.

title: Lower rank-one table lookups with higher-rank indices
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

Part of Gemma 4 support. This PR lets ingestion handle `aten.index.Tensor` when a 1-D checkpoint weight is indexed by an integer tensor with two or more dimensions. Before this change, ingestion supported only 1-D indices, so it rejected Gemma 4's mixture-of-experts router.

In Gemma 4, a router picks a few of many sub-networks ("experts") for each token, and `per_expert_scale[top_k_index]` reads one scale value for each selected expert. `per_expert_scale` has shape `[num_experts]` and `top_k_index` has shape `[tokens, top_k]`, where `top_k` is the number of experts picked per token.

## Background

- **Advanced indexing.** For a table of shape `[N]` and an integer tensor `indices`, `table[indices]` returns a tensor shaped like `indices`, where each element is `table[i]` for the corresponding index `i`. PyTorch calls this operator `aten.index.Tensor`.
- **Checkpoint weight.** A tensor loaded from the model's saved weights file. A **per-expert weight** has a separate tensor for each expert. An **expert view** is a read-only, zero-copy view that gives each token its routed experts' slices of a per-expert weight.
- **Loopy.** Ingestion's loop-level representation, which LoopyTron lowers to Tron IR and then to C++. **LoopyCheck** validates its types and storage. Loopy represents a tensor whose first axis is the batch of tokens, including runtime inputs such as token ids, as one row per token: `x[ix]` is the row for token `ix`, and `x[ix][j]` is element `j` of that row.

## Changes

1. **Translation.** For a 1-D checkpoint table and indices with two or more dimensions, `table[indices]` becomes `squeeze(embedding(reshape(table, [N, 1]), indices), -1)`: view the vector as an N×1 table, look up one row per index, then drop the trailing size-1 dimension. 1-D indices still map to `IndexSelect`. Unlike `IndexSelect`, `Embedding` accepts indices of any rank and already lowers to Loopy's table lookup, `Index`, which reads its table directly from a loaded checkpoint weight. Computed tables, per-expert weights and other model inputs are rejected with an error that names the kind of table found. With such indices, a table that is not 1-D gets its own error, as do 0-D and non-integer indices.
2. **Code generation.** A lookup into a 1-D table reads the weight directly and writes each result as one element of its output row, as in `out[ix][j] = table[indices[ix][j]]` for token `ix` and selected expert `j`. Each lookup reads its index as one value: a constant, a scalar variable, or one element of a row such as `topk`'s output or the token ids. Code generation proves from constants and loop bounds that an index read from a row stays within that row and, for a 1-D table, that the output element does too. The index value itself is not checked (see Index range).
3. **LoopyCheck.** A lookup into a 1-D table must produce a scalar, and a lookup into a 2-D table a row; other table ranks are rejected with a specific diagnostic. Writing a scalar lookup result into read-only storage (an element of a checkpoint weight or an expert view, including through slices) is rejected.
4. **Activation logging** (recording intermediate values for debugging) names the token embedding's output "Embedding". On main, every `Embedding` operation gets that name; now only one indexed by the input token ids, directly or through an unsqueeze, does.

`Note [Rank-one table lookups]` in `BulkLoopy.hs` documents how these stages fit together.

## Index range

Indices must be in `[0, N)`, as for `torch.index_select` and `torch.nn.functional.embedding`; negative indices, which PyTorch counts from the end, are not supported. Gemma 4's indices come from `topk` over the `num_experts` dimension, so they are always in range. The emitted C++ is a plain subscript, as on main, so an out-of-range index would read out of bounds.

## Not in this PR

Follow-up to this change:

- #4445: give the lookup its own operation, so the checkpoint-only restriction no longer has to live in translation.

Existing problems on main, unchanged by this PR:

- LoopyCheck accepts an `Index` into a per-expert weight, which the generated C++ cannot compile. This PR rejects per-expert tables only for the new lookup, in translation; a 2-D per-expert table reached through `aten.embedding` still passes LoopyCheck.
- #4739: Gemma 4 E-series models such as E4B also index their per-layer embedding by the input token ids, so its output is also logged as "Embedding".
- #4740: `IndexSelect` into a 1-D table, from `torch.index_select` or `table[indices]` with 1-D indices, fails late in lowering with an unclear message.
- #4438: LoopyCheck still accepts row-sized writes into expert views.
- #4442: outside lookups, reading one element of a single-row array is not bounds-checked.

## Testing

New cases in the existing ingest test suites cover translation (`FxTypedFxSpec`), code generation (`BulkLoopySpec`), the LoopyCheck rules (`LoopyCheckSpec`) and "Embedding" logging (`TypedFxBulkSpec`). The `BulkLoopySpec` cases check that a lookup over `topk` indices of width 1 and 8 reads index element `j` and writes output element `j` of the same token's rows. The `LoopyCheckSpec` cases that reject a row where a lookup needs one index now check the exact diagnostic.

Generated C++ for the build-test plugins is unchanged; none of them has a lookup into a 1-D table. The Gemma 4 trace that has one now gets past translation but stops later at an unsupported `Pow`, so no CI test compiles the lookup's C++ yet.

title: Share fused MoE routing inputs without copies
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

Part of Gemma 4 support. This PR lets the mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing step, which runs on the main thread, and a host-parallel kernel read the same top-k expert indices from one buffer, without copying it. #3271 builds on it to export Gemma 4's MoE layers through `moe_router`, ingestion's traceable MoE operation, whose lowering includes the routing step.

In an MoE layer, a router picks a few of many sub-networks ("experts") for each token. The top-k expert indices (`top_k_index`, shape `[tokens, top_k]`, where `top_k` is the number of experts picked per token) name the experts picked for each token. In Gemma 4 these indices have two readers: the routing step, and the per-expert scale lookup `per_expert_scale[top_k_index]` (#3267), which reads one scale per selected expert from the `[num_experts]` weight `per_expert_scale` in a host-parallel kernel.

On main, lowering from Loopy to Tron IR rejects a module in which routing and a host-parallel kernel read the same buffer, with a `Multiple consumers: ...` error. The error is avoided only when kernel fusion (a Loopy pass that merges adjacent host-parallel kernels over the same iteration space) merges the parallel read into the kernel that computes the indices, which leaves routing as the buffer's only reader. This PR handles the case in which the parallel read stays in its own kernel, for example because routing sits between it and that kernel.

## Background

- **Loopy and Tron IR.** Loopy is ingestion's loop-level representation. Lowering turns it into Tron IR, a statement-level representation that is then translated to C++.
- **Host-parallel kernel.** A loop over an iteration space, such as the token jobs of a batch (one job per token being processed), that generated C++ splits across host worker threads. The main thread is worker 0, and the other workers are helper threads. When helper threads exist, they process every item and the main thread processes none, but the main thread still takes part in the channel protocol (below) as worker 0.
- **Routing step (`MoeRoute`).** Reads the top-k indices of every token job and builds, for each expert, the list of tokens it processes. It runs only on the main thread.
- **Channel.** A synchronization object in generated C++ that guards one buffer. A phase is one round in which producers write the buffer and readers read it; the main thread starts each phase with `prepare`. Host producers publish item `i` with `finish_writing_at(i)`. Readers bracket their reads with `start_reading` and `finish_reading`, and wait for item `i` with `start_reading_at(i)`. The channel is set up with a writer count and a reader count, and the next `prepare` waits until that many writers and readers have finished the phase. For host-parallel and single-host readers, the producer decides when `start_reading_at(i)` returns: when a host-parallel kernel writes the buffer, the call returns once item `i` is published (per-item readiness).
- **Consumer contract.** Lowering classifies each read of a buffer, for example as host-parallel, single-host (main thread only, such as routing) or matrix-multiplication (a matrix-multiplication launch that takes the buffer as input), and combines all of a buffer's reads into one contract. The contract sets the channel's reader count and which threads call `start_reading` and `finish_reading`.

## Changes

1. **Consumer contracts.** Lowering now combines host-parallel reads over one iteration space with single-host reads, such as routing's, into a combined contract, with or without matrix-multiplication reads. On main it rejected this combination. A single-host read combined only with matrix-multiplication reads is still rejected.
2. **Channel synchronization for the combined contract.**
   - The channel counts one reader per worker, plus one per matrix-multiplication reader as on main. The single-host read adds no reader: the main thread is already worker 0 and makes its channel calls as worker 0.
   - Lowering emits one `start_reading`/`finish_reading` pair on every worker, spanning both reads in statement order. Helper threads skip routing and may finish reading before it runs. The main thread calls `finish_reading` only after routing, so the next phase cannot start while routing is still reading the indices.
   - Readiness still comes from the producer, as it does on main for a buffer that only routing reads. When a host-parallel kernel writes the indices, each parallel reader waits only for the items it reads, and routing waits for each token job's indices with `start_reading_at`.

The C++ channel runtime is unchanged.

## Testing

- `ingest/test/BulkLoopySpec.hs`: the consumer-normalization case now expects host-parallel plus single-host reads, with or without matrix-multiplication reads, to produce the combined contract instead of an error.
- `ingest/test/LoopyTronSpec.hs`: a new case lowers the MoE example with a host-parallel read of the indices after routing. It checks the combined contract, that the lowered module passes `TronCheck`'s channel-protocol check, per-item readiness, the reader count and routing's per-item wait.

title: Export Gemma 4 MoE through token-selective routing
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

Part of Gemma 4 support; stacked on #3270, and #3272 builds on it. This PR lets ingestion export Gemma 4's mixture-of-experts layers with `torch.export`. Upstream Transformers runs the selected experts with a data-dependent Python loop or with fused kernels, and ingestion can lower neither. This PR replaces only that step with `moe_router`, ingestion's traceable routing operation. Gemma's own router module, which scales its input, picks the top-k experts and multiplies their routing weights by learned per-expert scales, is unchanged.

The experts' gate and up projections stay fused. Each selected expert runs one gate/up matrix multiplication and splits the result into its gate and up halves, so the generated device code issues two expert matrix multiplications per selected expert (gate/up, then down). Separate gate and up projections, as in the existing `routed_gated_mlp` helper, need three.

## Background

- **Experts.** A mixture-of-experts layer holds many feed-forward sub-networks ("experts"). For each token, a router picks a few of them and blends their outputs using routing weights.
- **Gated feed-forward block.** Multiplies its input by a "gate" and an "up" projection, applies an activation to the gate, multiplies the two results, and maps the product back to the hidden size with a "down" projection.
- **Fused gate/up projection.** Gemma concatenates the gate and up projections into one matrix per expert, gate rows first. Transformers' `Gemma4TextExperts` stacks these for all experts as `gate_up_proj` with shape `[experts, 2 × intermediate, hidden]`, and `down_proj` as `[experts, hidden, intermediate]`.
- **`moe_router`.** A custom PyTorch operation that `torch.export` records as a single graph node. It takes a per-expert function, runs it only on the tokens routed to each expert, and sums the outputs weighted by the routing weights. Its pure-PyTorch implementation, `moe_router_eager`, runs during export-time numerical checks.
- **Reference inference.** Running the unmodified upstream model in Python to produce the logits that device output is compared against.
- **Checkpoint key template.** The per-expert tensor name that generated code loads, with `{}` replaced by the expert index, for example `model.language_model.layers.3.experts.{}.gate_up_proj`.

## Changes

1. **Expert export.** When exporting, but not during reference inference, this PR replaces `Gemma4TextExperts.forward` with a call to a new helper in `moe_export.py`, `routed_concatenated_gated_mlp`. The helper calls `moe_router` with the fused `gate_up_proj` and `down_proj` tensors and slices each expert's gate/up output into contiguous halves. Other models with fused gate/up experts can reuse it.
2. **Checkpoint templates.** The parameters stay stacked, so the existing export-metadata detection of stacked experts derives the templates `….experts.{}.gate_up_proj` and `….experts.{}.down_proj`, stored as `[out, in]`. No metadata code changes.
3. **Blend rounding.** Transformers has three expert implementations, selected by `config._experts_implementation`. `grouped_mm` and `batched_mm` sum the weighted expert outputs at the routing weights' precision (FP32) and round to the activation dtype once. `eager` rounds each weighted output before summing. The export rounds at the same points as the configured implementation.
4. **Shared `moe_router_eager`.** It now rounds each weighted contribution to the output dtype before adding it, matching upstream `eager`; previously it rounded the running sum after each addition. This applies to every model exported through `moe_router`. It still visits experts in ascending index order.
5. **Translation.** The rounding casts export as `aten._to_copy.default`. FX-to-TypedFx translation now handles it like `aten.to.dtype_layout`, with only `dtype` and `layout` keyword arguments.
6. **Blend-order note.** The C++ Note [MoE Blend Reduction Order] now states only that the device blend reduces in reverse routing-slot order. Gemma's per-expert scales can reorder weight magnitudes after top-k selection, so that order need not be smallest weight first. Comment only.
7. **Docs.** `ingest/README.md` describes the Gemma 4 MoE export: blend order, tolerances and eager-routing costs. It also notes that the export and runtime environments pin different Transformers versions, 5.15.1 and 5.12.1, whose Gemma 4 BF16 routers can pick different experts near ties, so reference outputs must come from the export environment.

## Checkpoint contract

A Gemma 4 MoE checkpoint consumed through this export stores, for each layer and expert `E`, `experts.{E}.gate_up_proj` with gate rows before up rows, and `experts.{E}.down_proj`, both as `[out, in]`.

## Not in this PR

- #4349: the device does not yet preserve the routing scores' FP32 precision; #3457, #3459 and #3463 add the explicit floating-point dtypes this needs.
- #4352: device output for the full A4B checkpoint still differs substantially from the reference.
- #4506: measuring the memory and time that the export and `moe_router_eager` use for the full 128-expert model.
- The generated Python reference model loads expert weights only through explicitly declared templates, not the derived ones above, so it cannot yet load Gemma 4 experts. GPT-OSS has the same limitation.

## Testing

`test_gemma4_export.py` compares exported programs with the upstream model in BF16 and FP32. It checks expert outputs against upstream `Gemma4TextExperts` under the `eager` and `batched_mm` implementations, with router input scales other than 1 and with top-1 and top-2 selection, and checks each layer's checkpoint templates and tensor orientation.

title: Add Gemma 4 A4B TP1, TP2, and TP4 execution
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

Part of Gemma 4 support; stacked on #3660. This PR adds Gemma 4 26B-A4B (26B parameters, about 4B active per token) as a model whose device code ingestion generates, runnable with 1-, 2- and 4-way tensor parallelism (TP1, TP2, TP4). Its runtime model names (slugs) are `ingested-gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`, `ingested-gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-tp2` and `ingested-gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-tp4`. Attention runs in generated kernels rather than Tron's dedicated attention hardware, which does not support this model's KV-cache geometry.

The default weights are a GPTQ checkpoint that stores each expert's gate and up projections as one fused tensor, matching #3271's export, which runs two expert matrix multiplications per selected expert instead of three. In a TP1 device comparison, one 24-token prompt generating 128 tokens, this combination took 7.67 ms per decode forward pass against 9.34 ms for separate gate and up projections (median of 3 runs). It issued 480 expert matrix multiplications per decode token instead of 720. Device logits were byte-identical between the two layouts on 3 test prompts.

**Merge is blocked** by #4349 and #4352: device output still differs substantially from the reference. The total variation distance (TVD) between next-token distributions, where 0 means identical and 1 means disjoint, reaches 0.98 at some positions. Merge is also blocked until the fused checkpoint is published under the exact name this PR uses (see Checkpoint contract).

## Background

- **GPTQ checkpoint.** Weights quantized to 4 bits in groups of input channels. Each quantized projection is stored as four tensors: packed weights (`qweight`), per-group `scales` and zero points (`qzeros`), and each input channel's group index (`g_idx`). GPTQ v1 and v2 differ in zero-point encoding: v1 stores each zero point minus one.
- **Tensor parallelism (TP).** Splitting each layer's work across 1, 2 or 4 FPGA slices. A slice is one FPGA with its memory and host CPUs.
- **Reference loader.** `load_patched_model` in `ingest/export/load_model.py`, which builds the upstream model for reference inference and export. Reference inference runs the upstream model in Python to produce the logits that device output is compared against.

## Changes

1. **Registry.** This PR adds a `gemma_4_a4b_it` entry to `config/models.yaml`, with the fused checkpoint as its default weights, and adds its three slugs to the CMake model-test selection.
2. **Fused expert loading.** For reference inference and export, the reference loader dequantizes each expert's fused `gate_up_proj` and its `down_proj` into Gemma's stacked expert tensors. It quantizes only the modules that the checkpoint stores as GPTQ, so the router projection stays unquantized. It rejects:
   - before loading, GPTQ checkpoints whose experts store `gate_proj` and `up_proj` separately, including the earlier split A4B checkpoint;
   - before loading, fused-expert checkpoints in any encoding other than int4 GPTQ v1;
   - after loading, checkpoints missing any expert tensor, the router weights, or any other weight the model needs.
3. **Shared GPTQ helpers.** This PR moves GPT-OSS's int4 GPTQ v1 dequantizer into `load_model.py` so that both models use it; GPT-OSS behavior is unchanged. Gemma GPTQ loads that configure no backend now default to GPTQModel's `torch` backend, so CPU reference runs do not auto-select an unpinned kernel from the Hub. Gemma checkpoints without GPTQ experts load as before.
4. **Generation tests.** Three FPGA tests, one per TP degree, share a helper. It first checks the generated model's structure: 30 attention layers, each with its own KV-cache slot, and 30 MoE routers over 128 experts with top-8 routing. It then compares device logits with logits from the original unquantized weights, allowing TVD above 0.10 at up to half the positions. TP2 and TP4 require at least 2 and 4 slices. The tests skip when the plugin is not built or the weights are unavailable.
5. **CI timing.** This PR adds runtime estimates for the three tests to `config/test-benchmarks.json`. They were measured with separate gate and up projections.
6. **Build.** The Nix package for GPTQModel, the GPTQ library Transformers uses to load these checkpoints, now declares its Ninja build dependency.

## Checkpoint contract

The published checkpoint must be named `_promoted/google--gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-ingest-best-gptq-fused--2026-07-07`, or both `config/models.yaml` and `t/gemma_4_a4b_generation.hpp` must change to its real name. It must be symmetric int4 GPTQ v1 with group size 64. It must store `experts.{E}.gate_up_proj.{qweight,qzeros,scales,g_idx}` with gate rows before up rows, plus `experts.{E}.down_proj.{…}`, and a BF16 router projection.

## Not in this PR

- #4349, #4352: device output accuracy, as described above.
- Publishing the fused checkpoint. CI exports from pinned public copies of each checkpoint's configuration and index files. A later PR in this stack adds that pin and the #4355 checkpoint staging that packaged ingestion needs at this layer. That PR's A4B entry still names the split checkpoint and must be repointed after publication.
- Re-measuring the CI timing estimates with the fused checkpoint.

## Testing

`test_gemma4_checkpoint.py` covers:
- fused expert assembly;
- the unquantized router;
- rejection of split, GPTQ v2 and incomplete checkpoints;
- the shared GPTQ v1 dequantization;
- quantizer settings kept for non-MoE Gemma checkpoints;
- the relocated GPT-OSS expert loader, which keeps its layout and biases.

`test_gemma4_export.py` checks that a Gemma 4 checkpoint saved without its vision-tower weights still loads for text and reproduces the full model's text logits. The new FPGA tests are `t_generate_ingest_1_gemma_4_a4b_fpga` and its TP2 and TP4 variants.

title: RoPE: add Ministral query-only amplitude scaling
author: ishapira-positron
body:
Add Ministral-3's query amplitude correction, 1 + beta * log1p(floor(position / original_context)), independently of frequency scaling. Rotary query lanes receive the product of the frequency attention factor and query scale; partial-rotary pass-through lanes receive only the query scale. Keys use the default disabled query strategy.

The existing llama4 strategy spelling follows Ministral-3's unshifted position formula; Transformers Llama 4 uses position + 1 and a different application site. Constructors require query parameters only when query scaling is enabled. Existing tests cover the context boundary, amplitudes, constructor constraints and partial-rotary lanes.

The stack adds Ministral ingestion and named-argument tool calling. Production use of rope_query_scaling::llama4 and llama4_rope_query_scaling_params in h/tron/kernels/rope.hpp is deferred to ishapira/ministral-04b-ir-serialize: ingest/src/LoopyTron.hs::mkRopeCfgType selects the template arguments and ropeCfgConstructorArgs emits the constructor parameters. Application-level query/key routing lands in ishapira/ministral-04e-eqsat-route.

Snapshot validation still requires the exact pinned completion-marker bytes; a rejection now reports the expected value and a bounded escaped prefix of the observed bytes to diagnose divergent cache views. This diagnostic does not repair or re-prime the cache.

Validation is tracked at each published head. A baseline-relative local gate pass still includes inherited hlint and formatting failures; it is not a clean Nix or CI success. Current model-cache and hardware outcomes remain separate required checks.

title: RoPE kernel tests: pin YaRN against Ministral's published parameters
author: ishapira-positron
body:
Checks the YaRN kernel with Ministral-3 parameters (head size 128, theta 1e6, factor 16, betas 32/1, original context 16384, truncated correction bounds) through `rope_cfg` and `scaled_rope_frequencies`. Eight scaled inverse frequencies are pinned against values evaluated outside Tron, in float32, with Transformers 5.15.1's `_compute_yarn_parameters`, together with their upper-half duplicates. Two sin/cos samples, read from the table `rope()` builds, cover the correction ramp (bin 30 at position 512) and the fully interpolated band (bin 40 at position 32768); their phases stay below 0.37, which keeps the stated 2e-5 absolute error budget.

Existing coverage does not catch what this case catches. None of the five YaRN-against-Transformers cases in t_fp32 uses this geometry: three are head 32 with untruncated bounds, one is head 64 with the GPT-OSS geometry, and "YaRN truncation snaps correction bounds to rotary bins" exercises `truncate=true` on `yarn_rope_scaling` directly with two hand-fed frequencies, never through `rope_cfg`. Truncation is what bin 30 discriminates: the bounds 20.385/36.440 snap to [20, 37], putting bin 30 at ramp 10/17 instead of about 0.599, so its scaled frequency moves 2.2% (0.000690702 against 0.000675329 untruncated), far outside the 2e-5 band. Bins 20 and 40 clamp to ramp 0 and 1 with or without truncation. Tests only; no production change.

title: Ingest export: share the helpers the Ministral-3 loader needs
author: ishapira-positron
body:
Centralize Ministral tokenizer correction in ingest/runtime/tron_ingest_tools/export.py::tokenizer_load_options. Its callers already exist here: torch_export.py::_export_model_impl, dump_intermediates.py::main, reference_logits.py::main and runtime/tron_ingest_tools/logit_test.py::load_hf_model_with_weights. #3905 adds TokenizerOptionsTest coverage, not a load_model.py caller.

Extend shared RoPE reference operations with attention-factor/query-scaling parameters, and forward them from apply_tron_rope on both its rank-3 and rank-4 paths. Batched-position cos/sin broadcasting is unchanged; only its comment now says why the padded table needs no further unsqueezing. These shared internals affect existing callers too. When query scaling is enabled, reject non-positive or NaN original_context with a runtime ValueError, including under optimized Python. Enable CTest before configuring ingest so later ingestion tests can register correctly.

The intermediate query-scaling API is superseded on #3906: rotation remains model-independent and apply_llama4_query_scale handles query amplitude separately. Generated callers of that standalone helper arrive in #3910 at ingest/src/BulkPython.hs::generateTernary and #3911 at ingest/src/TypedFxPython.hs::withQueryScaling.

title: prequant: Record a fixed aligned payload offset
author: ishapira-positron
body:
Set the prequant payload boundary to 4096 bytes and record it in `prequant_cache_header::payload_offset`. Header equality rejects entries with a different offset. Format version 3 skips the version used by an earlier on-disk layout.

This branch adds the offset and alignment constants and their existing header test coverage. The format and identity definitions come from `ishapira/prequant-01-format-key`; no cache entry is read or published here.

`kPrequantPayloadOffset` and the header field are consumed by `ishapira/prequant-02-io`, in `h/tron/hardware/prequant_cache.hpp::prequant_cache_reader::open`, and by the writer constructor in the same file on `ishapira/prequant-04-writer`. `ishapira/prequant-05-payload` uses `kPrequantDirectReadAlign` in that file's `read_payload_and_submit_regions` before enabling direct reads.

title: prequant: Publish complete cache entries atomically
author: ishapira-positron
body:
Add a streaming prequant-cache writer that publishes complete entries without retaining the whole tensor in memory. Each writer exclusively creates a staging file with a random nonce and trailing PID inside a held shard directory. Construction writes the header and zero-filled alignment gap; `write_fetcher` appends payload regions and records write failures.

title: Emit executable MoE Python references
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
Make generated Python references execute token-selective MoE routing and expert operations. `moe_view` materializes token-slot rows, and `moe_matmul` consumes those rows while preserving every trailing activation dimension returned by `F.linear`. Direct view-to-blend and pointwise expert-bias/projection compositions are covered for FP32/BF16, top-k 1/2, and rank-two/rank-three activations.

The TypedFx router matches the export helper's PyTorch dtype promotion, contribution rounding, and body-output accumulation dtype. Bodies needing promoted accumulation return that dtype; the caller rounds the completed blend. The Bulk blend helper models FP32 accumulation in reverse routing-slot order.

Bulk-to-Loopy preserves the mapping in the existing view representation. Pointwise expert bodies project a slot to its token when reading shared activation storage; direct matmuls retain the existing zero-copy token-slot view. A mapped view consumed directly by a blend is materialized into token-slot storage through the existing copy lowering. Channel waits follow the backing's index space.

A channel's parallel readers may now span several host-parallel iteration spaces, `QBatchItems` and `QBatchItemsExpertPairs`: each space keeps its own `ParConsumer`, and all of them read on the same host workers without adding participants; see Note [Parallel consumer iteration spaces] in `Tron.hs`. `normalizeConsumers` now takes consumers over `IterationSpaceF` so it can recognize those spaces, and it generalizes main's single host domain to a list, which has more than one entry only in this case. Aligned-lane readers keep main's rules: one iteration space, and no combination with parallel or single-host readers. Main's `consumerHostStripe` becomes `consumerHostStripes`, with `consumerHasHostStripe` for callers that only ask whether a consumer has a host stripe. Buffer reuse treats two such consumers as compatible when their matrix counts match and each stripe of either has the same lanes as a stripe of the other and a compatible iteration space. For single-stripe consumers this is main's check. `combineConsumers`' Haddock now points to Note [Parallel consumer iteration spaces] instead of repeating the combination rules documented at `normalizeConsumers`.

The direct view-to-blend case exercises the Bulk-to-Loopy boundary, full IR checking, and generated C++.

title: Add CLI tuning for Perfetto capture configurations
author: bretcraig-positron
body:
Generate validated Perfetto configs from CLI overrides for duration, categories, buffers, fill behavior, and periodic writes.

## Problem

Changing capture settings requires a separate Perfetto protobuf text (PBtxt) config. Manual edits are hard to reproduce. Perfetto validates them only when a capture starts, and they can change unrelated data sources or buffer routing.

## Solution

Add `perfetto/generate-config`. It reads a checked-in or custom PBtxt base with Perfetto v57.2's official `TraceConfig` schema. It applies only the requested `--categories`, `--exclude-categories`, `--buffer-kb`, `--fill`, `--duration-ms`, or `--write-period-ms` settings. Other settings stay unchanged. Each data source keeps its effective buffer routing, including named buffers. Buffer tuning affects all sources sharing TrackEvent's buffer. Invalid CLI overrides fail before capture starts.

`--write-period-ms 0` clears an inherited `output_path` along with the streaming fields; other overrides preserve it. V2 and shadow buffer limits account for native page rounding.

Without a leading `+`, category lists replace the corresponding base list and accept exact names or the standalone `*` selector. A finite `--categories` list disables unlisted C++ categories. It rejects inherited enabled tags other than `*`, which could bypass that restriction. `*` keeps wildcard selection.

A leading `+` appends every exact name in the list. For example, `--categories +memory,loading,driver-detail` adds all three categories to the base selection. `--exclude-categories +model,driver` extends the base exclusions and removes those exact names from the base enabled list so the exclusions take effect. Explicit enable/exclude conflicts still fail. Unsigned exclusion replacement still rejects a selector in the effective enabled list. Append mode rejects wildcards and per-name signs.

This example selects application categories. It also sets a 60-second duration and a 512 MiB TrackEvent ring buffer:

```bash
nix develop --accept-flake-config --command perfetto/generate-config runtron \
  --categories driver,sys,memory \
  --buffer-kb 524288 \
  --fill ring \
  --duration-ms 60000
```

The generator writes readable PBtxt or a binary config. One version in `flake.nix` selects the schema, capture tools, and Trace Processor. CMake pins the producer SDK to that release. The existing Nix Toolchain Contracts job tests config generation and release pin alignment. It runs on all GCP Nix workflow events, including draft PRs; Nix can reuse unchanged successful results. title: Add Perfetto CLI tuning to tronperf and wrapper
author: bretcraig-positron
body:
Let `nix run .#tronperf` and `nix run .#wrapper` tune Perfetto duration, categories, buffers, fill behavior, streaming, and OS events from the command line.

## Problem

`tronperf` and `wrapper` require users to choose or edit Perfetto PBtxt files to tune a capture. They also duplicate daemon lifecycle code and use fixed delays, so a workload can start before the launcher detects a failed capture. Both also write 0 to the kernel's `tracing_on` setting and never restore it, which stops other kernel tracing on the host.

## Solution

Connect [#4051's config generator](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4051) to both launchers. They now accept `--categories`, `--exclude-categories`, `--buffer-kb`, `--fill`, `--duration-ms`, `--write-period-ms`, and `--perfetto-config`. An unsigned finite category list restricts TrackEvent capture to the listed C++ categories. Custom bases with inherited enabled tags other than `*` reject that override.

A leading `+` appends every exact name in either category list; unsigned lists keep replacement behavior. For example, `--categories +memory,loading` adds both categories to the base selection. `--exclude-categories +model` extends the exclusions and removes the exact name `model` from the base enabled list. Explicit enable/exclude conflicts still fail.

The launchers also accept `--os-events` and `--os-buffer-kb`. These options add the checked-in `linux.ftrace` and `linux.sys_stats` sources without replacing the selected PBtxt config. Newly added events share a dedicated ring buffer. Original buffer routes are checked before append. Only effective base coverage removes an event from the added source.

The generator replaces `perfetto/compose-os-events`. Use `--os-events` for the checked-in sources. Put custom data sources in the selected base PBtxt.

Tune a runtron capture directly from its command:

```bash
nix run .#tronperf -- \
  --duration-ms 60000 \
  --buffer-kb 524288 \
  --fill ring \
  --categories driver,sys,memory \
  --output-file /tmp/runtron.trace \
  -m mixtral-8x7b-instruct-v0.1 -f myprompt.txt -l 256
```

Tune a rinzler capture, extend the base category lists, and add OS events:

```bash
nix run .#wrapper -- \
  -n rinzler \
  --duration-ms 15000 \
  --categories +driver-detail \
  --exclude-categories +model \
  --os-events \
  --os-buffer-kb 2097152 \
  -o /tmp/rinzler.trace
```

Shared launcher code generates a temporary binary config before changing the Linux tracing filesystem (tracefs). It waits for `traced` service readiness, `traced_probes` data-source registration, and client readiness before starting or signaling the workload. On exit, it stops and reaps the client before the daemons. Direct in-process `bin/runtron --trace FILE` captures are unchanged.

The launchers no longer write `tracing_on`. Perfetto v57.2 saves and restores it. A `linux.ftrace` source without `instance_name`, as in `sigusr1.cfg` or `--os-events`, still resets the primary tracefs instance, so another recorder there loses its buffered data. The capture guide lists what an ftrace session changes on the primary instance.

Daemon readiness waits for the complete native notification. Client readiness checks v57.2 service errors before starting or signaling a workload.

The wrapper runs its wait helper directly, without an intermediate shell that could leave a sleep process behind. An explicit `--duration-ms` or `-w` selects client-wait mode; a duration inherited from PBtxt does not.

OS-event generation keeps named ftrace instances separate from the unnamed default instance. If a daemon exits after reporting readiness, the launcher fails instead of reporting a partial trace as successful. A daemon that closes its readiness channel without reporting readiness fails instead of hanging the launcher.

## Testing

Commit `aba9085465` passed the focused Nix check with all 58 config and launcher tests, focused lint, all 23 workflow contract tests, and both public-app help checks.

Earlier, commit `b9d734cbe5` passed the focused Nix and lint gates and all 23 workflow contract tests.

- All 58 config and launcher tests passed in 24.2 seconds. A forced rebuild of the focused Nix check took 25.3 seconds on a warm build host. These times exclude GitHub checkout and cold-cache downloads. The check ran with fresh trust settings and import-from-derivation disabled. Existing tests now cover the new readiness failures, argument/stdin forwarding, and OS-source overlap.
- Both public Nix apps printed append-mode help. The Nix check exercised their config-generation paths and verified `PERFETTO_BIN_DIR` precedence.
- Host-only native checks completed two service-only captures, rejected an unsafe V2 size before daemon startup, and kept the workload gate closed in 100 service rejections. All owned children and temporary files were cleaned up. No FPGA workload, application producer, or OS-event overlay ran in these checks.

Before these fixes, twelve real captures used both public Nix apps with FPGA workloads. Recorded events and embedded configs verified appended categories, appended exclusions, restricted custom bases, and unsigned replacement. Every trace contained 32 completed forward passes, with no reported data loss. Eight invalid-input checks rejected settings without starting capture tools or starting or signaling a workload. These captures used existing v57.2 producer builds; no C++ rebuild ran. They did not test an OS-event overlay and were not rerun for these fixes.

Before that, commit `83509e5900` also passed the following checks:

The existing workflow suite and its ten validation cases passed, along with full CI machinery and lint Nix checks, CI-pin and guidance hooks, Ruff, Bash/shfmt, Nix formatting, and pinned Actionlint 1.7.12.
- Native v57.2 checks parsed five stock profiles and a tuned OS profile, observed service/probe/client readiness, and recorded 39,936 system-stat samples with no reported loss. Tracefs stayed unchanged, and all capture processes were reaped.

title: CI: cut CI machinery contracts runtime on builder-s
author: hvaneenoo-positron
body:
## Summary

- Evaluate all 13 source-invalidation fixture trees in one `nix eval` instead of 13 separate evaluations. Assertions are unchanged.
- Move the cold full-lint rebuild of an unformatted tree out of `test-lint-check-regressions.sh` into `test-lint-full-rejection.sh`. The CI machinery job starts it in the background after "Add Nix to PATH", so it overlaps the other steps. The final step, "Full lint rejection check result", runs even when an earlier step failed. On success it prints the log collapsed. On failure it prints the complete log expanded, adds an annotation with the check's failure message, and fails the job. The check is bounded by `timeout 300`. `test-background-check.sh` covers failure propagation and the expanded log. The fast regression script also gains a Lefthook `nixfmt` fixture.
- Build the `ci-machinery-contracts` Nix check as three parallel derivations behind the same check name. Tests and their whole-tree source input are unchanged.

This replaces the earlier version of this PR, which targeted the legacy `cmake-single-platform.yml`. The intent is the same (keep required CI machinery tests cheap), applied to `gcp-nix.yml`.

## Why

`CI machinery contracts` runs on `builder-s` for every GCP Nix run and was the largest `builder-s` consumer: 197 s median runtime and 38% of pool runner-hours from 21 to 23 September (2,006 runs). With 20 `builder-s` runners, run-start bursts queue Lint behind these jobs; Lint queue p95 was 23.5–31.8 minutes on those days.

Step times on a main run (`Test lint check regressions` 38 s, source invalidation 69 s) and a median PR run (Nix check 43.7 s):

| Change | Before | After (local) |
|---|---|---|
| Source invalidation | 69 s on `builder-s`, 28 s local | 3 s |
| Lint check regressions (foreground) | 38 s on `builder-s` | 5 s, plus the 31–33 s rebuild running in the background |
| `ci-machinery-contracts` Nix check, cold | 43.7 s median on `builder-s`, 60.9 s local | 30.2 s |

The expected job median is about 75–80 s on `builder-s`. `builder-s` runners have 8 vCPUs, and the builder image leaves Nix `max-jobs` at the default.

The background rebuild still runs on every PR, so coverage is unchanged. It competes for the runner's 8 vCPUs with the foreground steps; this PR's CI run will show how much that slows them.

## Validation

- `nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.ci-machinery-contracts --no-link --no-update-lock-file -L` (cold: 30.17 s split vs 60.86 s original)

title: Give placement strategies ownership of tile selection
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Placement strategies currently overwrite a shared table of device masks and its tile cursor. Router and expert overrides must save and restore that cursor to preserve the wrapped strategy's position. Give each strategy ownership of tile selection and remove the global `device_placer` entirely.

## Keep selection state in each strategy

`PlacementStrategy` exposes two operations: `begin_tensor(request)` identifies the logical tensor, and `next_tile_devices()` returns the devices that will store its next tile. Placement processes one tensor at a time; beginning another tensor changes what subsequent tile selections mean.

Rotating and shuffled placement keep their own counters. Router and expert wrappers retain the current tensor's override mode or device mask and delegate both operations only for tensors handled by their base. An override therefore leaves the base strategy's cursor untouched.

For example, ordinary tiles can select devices 0 and 1, an expert override can select device 0, and the next ordinary tile resumes at device 2. The earlier [expert-rotation fix](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4531) establishes this behavior using shared-cursor save/restore; this refactor preserves it through separate ownership.

## Compute cyclic masks directly

The [parent PR](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4536) extracts `cyclic_replica_mask` to fill the existing mask tables. This PR calls the same helper directly for each tile: it selects `replicas` consecutive positions starting at `rotation * replicas`, wrapping through the device set. Rotating placement retains its counter across tensors. Shuffled placement starts each tensor at the next rank from its existing seeded shuffle, then advances once per tile. This preserves the selection sequence without constructing or copying mask tables, making `device_placer` unnecessary.

## Preserve the loading boundary

`place_on_devices()` becomes a function with the same call syntax. It asks the installed strategy for the next tile's mask, intersects it with available devices, rejects an empty result, and records placement for logging. Standalone allocations still use the current device mask when no strategy is installed.

The strategy remains globally installed, and loaders still use `with_placement`. The method rename, unused shuffled-state cleanup, mutex removal, and cyclic-mask helper extraction precede this PR; the subsequent placement-context PR changes the owning scope and caller interface.

title: t/proxy runner skip semantics: strict CLI, all-skipped → exit 4, family selection (area-2 L3)
author: sthorup-positron
body:
## Where this PR sits

```
tt-01 .. tt-06            proxy scheduler, golden replay,
(merged)                  t/proxy test infra

    │
    ├───────────────────────────────┐
    ▼                               ▼

 area 1 (merged)            area 2 L1 (merged)
 capability contract         rinzler --port-file / --port 0

    │                               │
    └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                    ▼

          L2  launch-lifecycle (merged)
              readiness via the port file;
              pdeathsig; teardown redesign

                    │
                    ▼

          L3  skip-semantics — THIS PR
              strict runner CLI, replay outcome
              classification (any skip → failure),
              family selection at collection time

                    │
                    ▼

          L4  llama31-suites
              first replay modules, manifests,
              goldens, per-family CTest entries

                    │
                    ▼

          L5  oracle-tighten

                    │
                    ▼

          bench session (rows-only PR)
```

Completes the runner and collection contract the replay suites will run
under, before L4 adds the first real replay modules. The product problem:
a replay module whose module-scoped `suite` fixture skips on a missing
tokenizer dir made pytest exit 0, so missing required tokenizer files
could have reported PASS for a run that launched nothing. Such an
absence is a fault, not a supported mixed-weights host configuration:
the weights root is a fleet-wide mount. Based on `main`; no stack parent.

## Runner CLI: exactly three forms

`run_suite.sh` (reached as `gen/run_proxy_suite`) now accepts exactly
`test_rzproxy.py lib`, `<file>.py`, or `--family <family>`; anything
else — no target, extra arguments, a path or node selector, an unknown
mode, `test_rzproxy.py` without `lib` — exits 1 with a usage diagnostic
before any prerequisite check, so a mistyped CTest `COMMAND` fails instead of
skipping forever. Gate order: argument shape, target existence, and in
family mode the `suites/<family>/` directory (1), venv (4), family
module set (5 when empty — checked before the binary and weights
checks so their diagnostics cannot conceal a missing replay file set),
binary and weights root (1), then `exec` of `run_tests.py` in the
same PID. The raw venv exit 4 remains in every shell mode; only the
library CTest row maps it to SKIP, and future replay rows must omit
`SKIP_RETURN_CODE`. Lib mode bypasses the binary and weights gates and
keeps pytest's own skip semantics; the `TRON_PROXY_WEIGHTS_ROOT` test seam warns loudly
in every mode when active.

## Replay classification: `run_tests.py --replay`

The shell passes a private leading `--replay` (consumed in-process, never
seen by pytest) for every non-lib run. It attaches `ReplayOutcomes`, a
plugin that records pytest's reports and, once pytest itself returns 0,
classifies the run:

| Run shape | Exit |
|---|---|
| any reported item genuinely skipped | 1 |
| a module skipped at collection while others were selected | 1 |
| no item reported at all (`--collect-only`) | 1 |
| duplicate selected node IDs | 2 (before execution) |
| a selected item marked `xfail(run=False)` | 2 (before execution) |
| `--setup-only` / `--setup-plan` | usage error → 1 |
| otherwise | 0 |

A "genuine" skip is any skipped report without `wasxfail`; xfail and
non-strict xpass are outcomes of a test that executed, not skips.
`xfail(run=False)` never reaches the classifier: it is refused at
collection, unconditionally, because a replay item must execute.
The pre-existing usage-error remap (pytest 4 → 1) still runs first, so a
broken option can never masquerade as a skip. Library runs keep pytest's
verdict. Other nonzero pytest codes are preserved, including 5 when
nothing is collected or selected.

## Failure policy

Mark's first pass asked for a tighter policy than skip-when-all-skip.
Adopted: a replay entry requires its family's tokenizer files
under `/opt/positron/weights/huggingface` — one NFS mount shared by dev
boxes and CI test runners — and the built `rinzler_proxy`.
Replay suites need no FPGA and no model
tensors. The `suite` fixture FAILS on a missing tokenizer dir or binary;
the classifier fails a run over any genuinely skipped item (a tripwire
against skip creep) and has no exit-4 arm. An `xfail` marker covers only
what the test body does: anything raised in fixture setup or teardown
stays a failure, marker or not, so a prerequisite failure can never be
reported as XFAIL. The shell's binary and weights checks exit 1.
The shell venv gate retains raw exit 4 in all modes:
`t_proxy_lib` alone maps it to CTest SKIP for venv-less default hosts.

Family mode rejects a missing `suites/<family>/` directory before the
venv gate, so `--family lama31` exits 1 on every host. Nested-runner tests
copy `pyproject.toml` into the fake checkout to anchor rootdir and use
production addopts. Every runner diagnostic goes to stderr under an
`ERROR:` prefix and names the responsible node ID. L4 still owes
registration of `t_proxy_<family>` rows WITHOUT `SKIP_RETURN_CODE`; that
registration is not implemented by this PR.

## Family selection at collection time

Authoring contract, in `t/proxy/README.md` "Writing replay tests":

```python
from conftest import replay

@replay("chat")
def test_something(client, suite):
    ...
```

`replay(*tags)` wraps `pytest.mark.parametrize("suite", specs_with_tags(*tags), indirect=True)`;
`specs_with_tags` attaches a generated `replay_family` marker to every
param it returns, so manual parametrization with its output works the same
way. `conftest.py` registers `--family FAMILY`. A tryfirst wrapper on
`pytest_collection_modifyitems` checks, before `-k`/`-m` or any other
selector sees the items, that every collected item carries that marker
(an item without one ends the run with exit 2 naming the item), then
deselects other families' items. Other families therefore never produce
skip placeholders: a module whose tags match only another family
contributes zero selected items, a run in which every item is deselected
is pytest's own 5, and a globally dead tag still fails collection
whichever family was requested (`specs_with_tags` raises on an empty
selection). No private pytest API is used; the marker is registered in
`pyproject.toml`.

## Client isolation and the L3-owed lifecycle pins

The replay `client` fixture builds its HTTPX transport with
`trust_env=False`, so `HTTP(S)_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY` are ignored for
loopback replay traffic (the launcher's readiness probe already ignored
them); ownership is explicit — the SDK's `close()` closes a supplied
client (openai 2.41.1), and the outer HTTPX context covers the window
before the SDK takes ownership. The six lifecycle items the L2 review
deferred to this layer are discharged: restart on one `ProxyServer`,
the gap-stub serve loop, the already-running and binary-missing start
guards, the `/proc`-precondition and zombie-arm pins for the pdeathsig
observer, and the runner-contract extension.

## Tests

The `t_proxy_lib` row passes: **351 tests** at 88adc9b9b9. The
real-binary lifecycle case still skips only when the binary or tokenizer
is absent.

- **TestRunnerContract** (extended): real subprocesses over a relocated
  fake checkout drive every CLI rejection (parametrized malformed
  invocations), the gate order, the family exit-5 arm, the unknown-family
  rejection, lib-mode propagation, and the ambient weights-override
  scrub and warning, plus a rootdir pin that plants a decoy `pytest.ini`
  above the fake checkout and asserts the nested node IDs stay short.
- **TestReplayOutcomes**: module-fixture skip → 1 naming every item
  (the product failure; the production `conftest.py` `suite` fixture
  now FAILS outright on an absent tokenizer dir under
  `launch.WEIGHTS_ROOT`; the test checks that absence when run), partial
  → 1 naming the item, call-phase xfail family → 0, fixture setup and
  teardown failures stay failures under xfail markers, an
  xfail(run=False) item is refused before execution (2), teardown skip
  counts, teardown error behind a skip stays a failure, collection skip
  → 1 (or 5 when alone), collect-only and setup-only handling with and
  without `--replay`, duplicate node IDs → 2, library skips keep pytest
  semantics. Single-use synthetic modules are inlined at their test.
- **TestFamilySelection**: three `@replay` usages (decorator on a test,
  `pytestmark`, and a class) × two families with a `suite` override that
  RAISES for the other family (so the pass count proves selection),
  family without matching suites → 5 (including the `@`-prefixed-family
  argfile pin), dead tag → 2, an item without family metadata → 2 with an
  absent family too, duplicates judged after deselection, membership
  error wins over the duplicate check, and the family-mode `--replay`
  handoff through the shell (all-skipped family run → 1, deselected
  family neither skipped nor named).
- **TestClientIsolation**: the production `client` fixture under a
  nested pytest with only `suite` overridden, proxy env vars pointed at
  a refusing port and `NO_PROXY` blanked, closed state observed from a
  later test for a passing and a failing consumer alike.
- **TestProxyLifecycle / TestPdeathsig** additions: restart, gap serve
  loop, start guards, `proc_state` precondition and zombie arm.

The nested runs pin `PY_COLORS=0`, scrub `PYTEST_*`/`PYTHON*`/coverage
variables, match pytest's summary line in a warning-proof form, and
pin the copied `pyproject.toml` as the nested rootdir anchor.

## Docs

`t/proxy/README.md` gains "Writing replay tests" (the `@replay` contract),
the three-form CLI, the gate order, the exit-code list (0–5) as the one
place the codes are stated, the failure policy as the rules behind those
codes, and the proxy environment note. `run_suite.sh`, `run_tests.py`,
`t/CMakeLists.txt`, `GNUmakefile` and `t/README.testing.md` each keep one
sentence and a pointer to it.
The per-family CTest naming (`t_proxy_<family>`) replaces the earlier
`t_proxy_harmony` placeholder; the gpt-oss/harmony port is deferred
beyond L4 with no promised CTest name.

## Review

Three planning-doc review rounds (multi-model panel; 14 + 12 + 10
findings, all folded into the plan before implementation). Code round 1
on the full branch: 1 P1 (the family-mode `--replay` handoff had no
test — the one shape CTest will ever run), 2 P2s, 11 P3s; the P1, both
P2s and six P3s fixed as three commits, the rest declined under the
repo test policy or recorded. Re-review of those fix commits (fresh
adversarial whole-branch read + incremental panel): no P0/P1, 1 P2 +
6 P3s, all taken as two more commits. A capers review of the
Mark round found one P1 (xfail masking a prerequisite failure), five P2s
and nine P3s; the P1, the P2s and four P3s land as eight fix commits on
top, including the setup and teardown fixes (1e0d3cae68 / 47c570e20b); the
rest are recorded. A re-review of those eight commits found no P0/P1; its
two P2s (the run=False hole and the draft refresh) and seven P3s land as
five more commits.

Mark's second round asked for the family-membership check to stop
depending on pytest internals and, more broadly, for less machinery.
Taken as: `@replay(...)` + a generated marker replace the
`get_direct_param_fixture_func` inspection and the canonical-path
validation (2f7767ea51); the six smaller comments (c69e4815b9); the exit
codes stated in one place (043588974d). A fresh whole-branch review then
focused on over-engineering and readability: no P0/P1; taken as four
commits that remove seven redundant nested-pytest test rows, inline a
one-caller helper, drop a fixture-phase `pytest.xfail()` exclusion and
the family-glob's LC_ALL/failglob/noglob hardening (nothing produces
those inputs), inline single-use synthetic modules at their tests, and
point every runner comment at the README instead of restating it
(fb8c80626c..b76fed7ce0, −241 lines in `t/proxy`).

## Heads-ups / residuals

- **Family-mode exit 5 remains meaningful**: with an existing family
  directory and the venv gate passed, no replay modules means 5; pytest
  also retains 5 when family selection leaves no items. An unknown
  family directory now fails earlier with 1. The first family entry
  (`t_proxy_llama31`) lands with L4 together with the modules it runs,
  WITHOUT `SKIP_RETURN_CODE`. `make test-proxy`'s configure-only
  prerequisite must become the proxy build target at that point.
- **Bench rows**: the genoa96 `t_proxy_lib` row is refreshed at
  88adc9b9b9 (6.1 s on main → 24.1 s, 59 MB: the
  nested-runner tiers pay real venv subprocess starts). The genoa32 row
  stays stale pending a genoa32-class host; it rides the planned bench
  session.
- **Declined test rows** (recorded, not taken): several message-pinning
  shell arms, the `session.testsfailed` guard, and the glob-hardening
  scenarios removed above (inherited `SHELLOPTS`/`BASHOPTS`) — revisit
  only if a producer appears.

title: Split software attention pages across cores by query (for small page and large query counts)
author: BillBaumann
body:
Parallelize software attention within a page when hardware offload or sliding windows leave too few pages to keep cores busy. Workers process disjoint query ranges in both Ready and Pending phases, preserving each query's full-page reduction and section-completion accounting.

Split only single-page sections with at least 32 relevant queries, when productive page/KV-head tasks number at most half the workers. The planner accounts for worker load, speed, and setup/join overhead; it requires a 10% predicted improvement and chooses the fewest pieces within 3% of the best predicted completion time.

Measured GPT-OSS prompt throughput improves **2.38% at 2K** and **4.28% at 32K**; generation improves **1.03% at 32K**. Llama controls are equivalent to main in both phases. Changes under 1% are reported as equivalent.

| Model | Users / instances | Prompt / gen tokens | Prompt throughput | Gen throughput |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| GPT-OSS 120B TP4, HW attention on | 1 / 1 | 2,049 / 128 | +2.38% | equivalent |
| GPT-OSS 120B TP4, HW attention on | 1 / 1 | 32,769 / 128 | +4.28% | +1.03% |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP4, handwritten | 8 / 2 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP2, handwritten | 8 / 4 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |

Tests cover Ready/Pending splits, sliding windows, query coverage, completion accounting, and cases where splitting should be declined.

title: Preserve MoE router precision with per-plugin placement
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

On main, generated plugins compute the mixture-of-experts (MoE) router's linear layer, the *gate*, on the FPGA with INT4 weights, whose quantization can change a token's experts. This PR lets a plugin compute the gate on the CPU from BF16 weights.

`ingest.moe_router: cpu|fpga` in `config/models.yaml`, or `--moe-router`, sets placement per plugin. Under the default, `fpga`, the 20 plugins compared generate headers and traces byte-identical to main's. GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3-30B-A3B ("Qwen3") switch to `cpu`. GPT-OSS-20B gets a lower mean total variation distance (TVD) and 4.6-5.5% faster decode per user. Qwen3 gets a 12.6% shorter time to first token and 2.1% faster decode.

It adds no thread pool or TBB; an earlier revision's router pool, placement pass, launchers and `cpu` default are gone. This PR and #4366 can merge in either order.

## Background

- **Workers.** A *pass* is one call of the generated `run()` over n tokens. It runs on the main thread plus H *helpers*, which stripe host kernels' tokens round-robin, and A ≥ 1 *attention workers*, which otherwise wait for attention jobs.

## Changes

1. **Router matvec kernel** (`h/tron/tensor/weight_matrix.hpp`, `h/tron/kernels/host_matvec.hpp`). Each router matrix is stored as packed BF16 when every element is in a safe range, else as exact FP32 ([Note [Host MoE router matvec]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/h/tron/tensor/weight_matrix.hpp#L27), [Note [BF16 matmul range]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/h/tron/kernels/host_matvec.hpp#L23)). `matvec` picks BF16 or FP32 per token, independent of the pass and thread. Exact FP32 alone would match precision, as in the handwritten Mixtral router (`h/tron/models/feed_forward.hpp:116`); packing halves the bytes and uses the AVX-512 BF16 dot instruction. Packed rows are a `const_view` over `padded_row_major`; `btensor` does not fit, since it allocates each row separately in the DMA heap. [Note [BF16 bits through float]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/h/common/numerics/bf16.hpp#L75) records a clang hazard these kernels avoid.
2. **`MatVec` op and code generation** (`ingest/src/{Ops,LoopyTron,LoopyCheck,Tron,TronCpp,TronCheck}.hs`, `ingest/src/Bulk*`). `MatVec` multiplies each token's row by a weight in the new `HostMatrix` memory space, which TronCpp emits as a `weight_matrix` ([Note [Kernel matrix-vector products]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/ingest/src/Ops.hs#L58), [Note [HostMatrix weights]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/ingest/src/Tron.hs#L484)). Router weights from an FP32 checkpoint or `--synthesize-missing-tensors` load as FP32 with one warning.
3. **Gate recognition and policy** (`ingest/src/RewriteFx*`, `ingest/src/TypedFx*`, `ingest/Main.hs`). A pre-scan finds each `MoeRouter`'s gate `Linear` through its top-k; a per-gate EqSat rule relabels it `MoeGateLinear` ([Note [MoE gate recognition]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/ingest/src/RewriteFxRewriteFx/EqSat.hs#L1220)). `fpga` lowers it like `Linear`; `cpu` lowers it to `MatVec` plus bias, which fusion merges with the RMSNorm and top-k into one *router kernel* ([Note [MoE router placement policy]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/ingest/src/TypedFxBulk.hs#L497)).
4. **Aligned lane domain** (`ingest/src/LoopyTron/{LaneDomain,LivenessAnalysis,BufferReuse}.hs`, `ingest/src/{Tron,TronCheck,TronCpp,TraceSidecar}.hs`, `h/tron/models/{aligned_lanes,model}.hpp`). The router kernel and the token-striped kernels linked to it through CPU-written rows (the *domain*) share one stripe ([Note [Aligned lane domain membership]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/ingest/src/LoopyTron/LaneDomain.hs#L24), [Note [Aligned lane domain]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/ingest/src/TronCpp.hs#L1693)). Lane-side channel ends (`LaneP`, `LaneC`) make liveness and buffer reuse add a channel wherever a row changes stripe. Under `cpu`, buffer reuse keeps channel prepares out of the router-to-expert window ([Note [Prepares around the MoE router]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/d296e54f278fae3e570f1cc38aad086179f851f6/ingest/src/LoopyTron/BufferReuse.hs#L219)).
5. **Config and build** (`config/{models.yaml,model_definitions.py}`, `ingest/{build-model.py,build-all.sh,CMakeLists.txt,README.md,tron-ingest.cabal}`, `bin/ci/model-plugins/generate.py`). `build-model.py` rejects a `--moe-router` contradicting the registry.
6. **Tests** (`t/`, `ingest/test/`, fixtures in `ingest/src/Loopy.hs`, `config/test*`, `bin/ci/model-plugins/test_generate.py`) cover the kernel, the lane rule and each TronCheck invariant.

## Lane rule

A domain kernel stripes a pass's n tokens over L(n) lanes (previously L = H):

```
L(n) = 1       if H = 0          (the main thread runs them)
L(n) = H       if H ≥ 1, n ≤ 2H
L(n) = H + A   if H ≥ 1, n > 2H
```

Attention workers join large passes because helpers alone are too slow for Qwen3's router. With n ≤ 2H they would own at most one token each, so they sit out. `reset_channels` sets channel participant counts once per pass with `tron::attention_lanes_join`, built on the helpers' `tron::aligned_lanes`, so counts always match the stripe; a counted thread that skipped a round would hang the others. Attention workers run domain work in the main thread's order, which rules out deadlock.

## Accuracy

`t_generate_ingest_1_gpt_oss_20b` measures TVD from Hugging Face logits at 20 positions:

| GPT-OSS-20B router | Mean TVD | Largest TVD | Positions above 0.10 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FPGA, INT4 (main) | 0.0523 | 0.107 | 2 |
| CPU, BF16 (this PR) | 0.0482 | 0.166 | 1 |

Position 3 worsens from 0.104 to 0.166 (cause unknown) but stays within the test's unchanged limits.

## Throughput

Main (`1feddd0dcd`) against an earlier build of this PR (`89dec66602`). Each user sends a 2,048-token prompt and generates 512 tokens. Each entry is the median of six paired `runtron` runs, and in every entry all six pairs moved the same way.

| Configuration | Time to first token | Decode speed per user | Total output rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-OSS-20B, 1 user, 2 cards | 1.8% shorter | 4.6% faster | 3.7% higher |
| GPT-OSS-20B, 1 user, 4 cards | 2.3% shorter | 5.5% faster | 4.5% higher |
| GPT-OSS-20B, 4 users, 4 cards | 3.1% shorter | 4.6% faster | 3.7% higher |

Qwen3's result depends on expert placement. Under main's former placement, each expert's gate, up and down projections landed on one card with the CPU router, and Qwen3 decoded 5.2% slower than with the FPGA router. #4685, now on main, places experts by a uniform plan when there is no load profile. With that placement, Qwen3 with 4 users on 4 cards is faster with the CPU router than with the FPGA router: time to first token 12.6% shorter, decode 2.1% faster, total output 6.8% higher (both routers in one binary, all six pairs agreeing).

Per token, packed router weights are 1.7–2.4× faster than FP32 storage while they are in cache, and equal when read from DRAM. On the timed configurations, FP32 storage would cost an estimated 0.4–1.2% of GPT-OSS-20B decode.

## Not in this PR

- The router kernel copies #4366's FP64 accumulator merge, with a TODO to share it. `tron::dot` is unchanged, so this PR no longer fixes #4371.
- #4366's per-position TVD cap of 0.13 is below position 3's 0.166; a later PR re-derives the limits after both merge.
- GPT-OSS-120B and Mixtral stay on `fpga`, unmeasured; Gemma-4 A4B does not ingest on main.
- Sigmoid and group-limited gates stay `Linear`, which fails ingestion under `cpu`.
- Kernel names change in `cpu` plugins, so Perfetto queries keyed on the old names need updating.

## Testing

- GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3 router outputs and greedy tokens match, bit for bit, plugins hand-edited to this design before the lowering existed.
- TSan on GPT-OSS-20B reports only a pre-existing teardown race. TSan cannot see AVX-512 row accesses.

Refs #4374.

title: Validate raw tensor latch payload alignment
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Tensor latches that watch a payload's own final 8-byte word now assert, at bind time, that the word is 8-byte aligned, and the open TODO about their size-only constraint is replaced with the contract they rely on.

## Problem

`tensor_latch<block_producer_t>` and the ptensor latch signal readiness through the payload itself:

- `bind()` points `trigger` at the last 8 bytes of the payload, or of each result tile for ptensor.
- `fill_nans()` sets that word to an all-ones NaN marker.
- The consumer uses `mwaitx` to wait until the producer's final store changes it.

This depends on the word being overwritten by a single 8-byte store that the consumer sees all at once. That only holds if the word doesn't straddle a cache line.

The existing `requires` clause only checks that the payload's byte size is a multiple of 8. Whether the final word is aligned also depends on where the storage starts, which is what the TODO above `bind()` asked. Suppose the payload started at an address that isn't a multiple of 8 (a hypothetical):

1. The final word would straddle a cache line, so the producer's store to it is not guaranteed to be atomic.
2. The consumer could see the word half-overwritten.
3. A half-overwritten marker already compares unequal to the marker, so the consumer would treat the payload as ready and read it before its last bytes are written.

This risk comes from reading the code. Every tensor type latched today has storage aligned to at least 8 bytes, and ptensor tile boundaries fall on multiples of 128 elements, so no current instantiation hits it.

## Approach

Each `bind()` now asserts `is_aligned(end, sizeof(uint64_t))` just before it derives the trigger from `end`. The ptensor latch checks every tile's end, because each tile's final word is watched separately. The check has to run at runtime: `dmatensor` payloads are heap-allocated, so their address isn't known at compile time. `TRON_ASSERT` is always enabled. `bind()` runs once per item each time a per-item channel resets, so the cost is one mask-and-branch per watched word.

The comment above `bind()` now states the contract in place of the TODO:

- The latch checks that the final word is aligned.
- The producer is still responsible for writing that word atomically, last, and only after the rest of the payload is visible. That part stays unchecked.

title: Fix NaN marker test coverage for all scalar formats
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

  The NaN-marker test silently skipped bf16, fp16, and float: its loop bound, sizeof(T) / sizeof(uint64_t), evaluates to zero for those types. Only double exercised the assertions, despite the production
  comment citing this test as verification for all four formats.

  Decode the 64-bit marker into a typed array with std::bit_cast and check every element. This verifies that each marker is a NaN and differs from the arithmetic NaN produced by inf - inf, increasing focused
  coverage from 2 to 22 assertions. It also removes pointer type-punning from marker decoding and diagnostic logging.
