title: ingest: Separate routing and scalar references in size types
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Size and iteration-space types currently force routing references and numeric bounds to share the same name type. This PR separates those representations so later lowering changes can resolve each
  appropriately, while preserving existing behavior.

  ## Why separate the references?

  An iteration space describes the indices a loop or channel covers. Its references can serve different purposes: `TokenSlot routing top_k` identifies a mixture-of-experts routing object, while `VarSize
  extent` supplies a numeric bound for a `Fin` iteration space.

  Previously, both references had type `Name k`. Choosing a routing-specific namespace therefore also constrained numeric bounds to that namespace. The types could not express routing names alongside scalar
  expressions resolved from configuration values or local variables.

  ## Independent parameters, compatible aliases

  Introduce `SizeVarF k a`: known dimensions retain their `Name k` references, while `VarSize` carries an independently chosen payload `a`. `IterationSpaceF k a` carries that distinction through its `Fin`
  bound, preserving the existing size algebra.

  Keep the existing types as aliases:

  ```haskell
  type SizeVar k = SizeVarF k (Name k)
  type IterationSpace k = IterationSpaceF k (Name k)
  ```

  Existing consumers therefore retain their representations. Pretty-printing accepts the generalized scalar payload, and constructor imports move to the new data types. Lowering and C++ generation remain
  unchanged.

  This is the first prerequisite in the stack. Channel-payload traversal follows in #4450; scalar-bound and routing-name resolution are handled by later layers.

title: ingest: Traverse channel iteration-space payloads
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Channel producer and consumer types hard-code Loopy iteration spaces, tying liveness analysis and lowered Tron declarations to the same representation. This refactor makes their iteration-space payload configurable and traversable, preparing lowering to transform that payload while preserving the surrounding channel contract.

  ## Transform iteration spaces through channel roles

  `Producer k`, `ConsumerDomain k`, and `Consumer k` now take the complete iteration-space payload as a type parameter and derive `Functor`, `Foldable`, and `Traversable`.

  For example, a mixed consumer contains both `MatrixConsumer count` and `ParConsumer space`. A subsequent lowering pass can use `traverse lowerIterSpace` to transform `space` while retaining the matrix count and consumer structure. The same operation handles parallel producers and leaves roles without an iteration space intact.

  Parameterizing the complete iteration space keeps reference resolution in the iteration-space lowering function; channel roles only provide traversal through their structure.

  ## Preserve behavior while preparing the lowering boundary

  Loopy liveness analysis and buffer reuse explicitly retain `Size.IterationSpace Loopy`. Tron declarations and kernels use a new `Tron.IterationSpace` alias, which still denotes that same representation. Consumer normalization, channel synchronization, and generated C++ retain their existing behavior.

  The parent PR, #4449, separates routing and numeric references within iteration spaces. This layer makes their channel containers traversable; subsequent PRs use that capability to resolve scalar bounds and routing names during lowering.

title: ingest: Resolve numeric loop bounds in lexical scope
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Finite loop bounds can reference configuration values or enclosing loop indices. This PR resolves those references when lowering Loopy to Tron, so C++ generation uses the declared configuration field or local variable.

## The bug, with an example

`Fin n` describes the integer indices from zero up to, but excluding, `n`. Its bound can be a symbolic size expression containing named numeric values.

Consider this Loopy program, written as pseudocode:

```text
config extent = head_dim  // emitted as the model field head_size

for i in Fin(extent):
    for j in Fin(i):
        ...
```

Before this PR, LoopyTron copied these iteration spaces into Tron without resolving their numeric references. The C++ size renderer then turned each reference into a bare identifier using its original Loopy spelling:

```cpp
for (size_t i = 0; i < extent; i += 1) {
    for (size_t j = 0; j < i; j += 1) {
        // ...
    }
}
```

There is no C++ variable named `extent` here. The configuration value lives at `model.head_size`. With this PR, the outer condition becomes `i < model.head_size`; the inner condition remains `j < i`, with `i` resolved to the enclosing loop's local variable.

The configuration value in the regression test is known at ingestion time. The problem is resolving a named bound correctly, even when its value is constant.

## How the fix works

The preceding PRs introduced separate parameters for routing names and numeric references, and made channel producers/consumers traversable. This PR uses that groundwork to change Tron's iteration-space payload:

```haskell
-- Before: numeric references are still Loopy names.
type IterationSpace = IterationSpaceF Loopy (Name Loopy)

-- After: numeric references are resolved Tron expressions.
type IterationSpace = IterationSpaceF Loopy KernelExpr
```

For a numeric reference, lowering produces either `KernelConfig` for a configuration field or `KernelVarExpr` for a local index. `kernelSizeName` reuses ordinary kernel-expression lookup and rejects references to non-scalar objects.

The implementation has two entry points because the available environments differ:

- **`lowerIterSpace`** runs while lowering declarations and top-level statements. It obtains configuration bindings from the LoopyTron state. Buffers, channels, and parallel kernels use this path.
- **`kernelIterSpaceFor`** runs inside a kernel body. It uses the current kernel environment, which also contains enclosing loop indices. A nested `For` resolves its bound before adding its own index binding; that new index is in scope in the body.

Both use `Size.traverseIterationSpace`, which accepts separate callbacks for routing references and numeric references. This PR uses `pure` for routing references and lowers the numeric references. `lowerProducer` and `lowerConsumer` are simply `traverse lowerIterSpace`.

Finally, `sizeToCppWith` lets C++ generation render each resolved numeric reference through `kernelBodyExpr`. That supplies the existing rules for `model.<config>` access and local-variable lookup. The surrounding symbolic sums, products, and known dimensions stay intact: buffer resizing still inspects that structure, for example to recognize a multiple of `BatchSize`.

## Relationship to the routing-name PR

This fixes an existing numeric-bound emission bug independently of #4244. It also gives #4244 a traversal that distinguishes numeric references from routing references, including routing metadata nested inside a `Fin` size. The subsequent PR can then resolve routing names without treating a numeric bound such as `extent` as an MoE routing object.

The changes to buffer and channel construction carry the new iteration-space representation across the Loopy/Tron boundary. General support for dynamically sized `Fin` buffers remains outside this change; their existing allocation restrictions still apply.

## Validation

The new case in `LoopyTronSpec` checks that the input passes `LoopyCheck`, then checks the generated C++ for both `i < model.head_size` and `j < i`. It fails on the parent because the outer bound is emitted as bare `extent`.

During the stack split, the regression was run against the parent, and the full `ingest-tests` suite passed with this fix: **1,080 tests, zero failures**. `bin/ingest-cabal build all` also passed. The test belongs to the existing ingestion suite run by CI.

title: Allocate sliding-window KV storage in independent chunks
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
The key/value (KV) cache stores attention keys and values for earlier tokens. A sliding-window attention layer needs only a bounded recent history, but allocating its storage for an entire logical book can require a large allocation before most of that capacity is populated. A **book** is the scheduler's group of consecutive token pages; each page contains 64 tokens.

Separate sliding storage into independently allocated, whole-page **chunks**. Each allocation targets at most 256 MiB, except when one page exceeds that size. For example, a layout with 50 MiB of sliding storage per page uses five-page chunks: 320 tokens and 250 MiB of data, rounded to 256 MiB by the allocator.

### Behavior

- Allocate chunks as appends need them. Reserve storage before publishing tokens and prevent compaction from changing offsets during reservation. A failed reservation releases only that attempt's allocations and preserves existing data.
- Keep page objects stable and address data relative to its chunk, including a shorter final chunk. Logical book capacity is bounded by the aggregate byte count of each retention group (full-history or sliding-window storage) and the embedding buffer. Full-history attention storage uses whole-book buffers.
- Restore missing populated storage transactionally before recomputing its keys and values. Failed or cancelled restoration preserves resident neighboring chunks and separately reserved suffix storage. Unused tails need no restoration.
- Account for resident bytes added to existing books, including allocations retained by an active reference after an append fails. Capture resident bytes before relocation removes a book from the cache's accounting.

This PR provides storage allocation and accounting. [#4456](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4456) uses the chunk boundaries to reclaim expired history within active books; [#4466](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4466) adds memory-aware admission.

### Validation

Validated on Andoria (`andoria-d03d`), based on `main` at `98bb8cb22f947574c6a2f36abd807e1e747d4916`. Formatting and the real Rinzler build passed.

On the storage/reclamation parent `d98e0ea0984ed4de69d1ae94cd40f2465d30ba6b`, `t_llama_unit` passed 209,403 assertions across 43 cases and `t_heterogeneous_scheduler` passed 1,900 across two cases. Both suites also passed with the admission layer applied.

The complete stack passed `make build-test`. `make test-host` reported 82 passes, one skip, and one failure. The selected profile omits five model fixtures required by `t_chat_template` (Mixtral 8x7B, Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 2 9B, GPT-OSS 120B, and GPT-OSS 20B). `t_proxy_lib` skipped because its virtual environment was absent. These are the same profile limitations observed before the review fixes; no assertions were weakened.

Existing required host CI suites cover addressing across chunk boundaries, allocation-failure cleanup, restoration, cache accounting, and append retries that permit compaction. No dedicated CI job is added.

title: Reclaim expired sliding-window KV chunks within active books
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
An active request can retain expired sliding-window key/value (KV) data when newer tokens occupy the same book. A **book** is the scheduler's group of consecutive token pages; each page contains 64 tokens. Sliding-window attention needs a bounded recent history, while full-history attention needs the entire preceding sequence.

Use the independent storage **chunks** from [#4455](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4455) to reclaim expired sliding history within a book that remains in use. A chunk is a separately allocated, whole-page portion of that storage.

### Behavior

- Record the token position protected by each retained sequence handle and pending query. A **pin** is a scheduler reference that protects needed history. Saved positions remain meaningful when token-tree edges split or merge.
- Release a chunk only when all populated tokens lie outside every protected history requirement. Protect the widest active sliding window plus one token and one 64-token page. Use conservative book boundaries for unknown positions and shared branches. Unused tail allocations can be released independently.
- Reclaim on the scheduler worker between model forwards, when no forward operation can access released storage. Check memory pressure before extending storage and after completed forwards.
- Restore missing storage only when a query or required recomputation needs it. A cache hit at a resident book suffix can avoid restoring expired earlier chunks. Remove the obsolete whole-book traversal helper.

**Restoration** allocates missing storage before recomputing its keys and values. A book needing restoration reserves all missing populated chunks and any preceding history needed for recomputation transactionally. Readiness and recomputation operate on whole books, so an old-prefix request can still require a substantial temporary allocation. Full-history storage remains resident.

This is the middle layer of the stack. [#4466](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4466) limits new work using estimated host-memory demand.

### Validation

Validated on Andoria (`andoria-d03d`), based on `main` at `98bb8cb22f947574c6a2f36abd807e1e747d4916`. Formatting and the real Rinzler build passed. At parent `d98e0ea0984ed4de69d1ae94cd40f2465d30ba6b`, `t_llama_unit` passed 209,403 assertions across 43 cases and `t_heterogeneous_scheduler` passed 1,900 across two cases.

The FPGA reclamation test previously passed without skipping: 238 assertions across two cases on `SYSTEM_CONFIG="--instance 1,4"`. Since that run, the reclamation layer only removes an unused helper; the reclamation behavior and assertions are unchanged.

title: ingest: Separate MoE router identity from storage
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
MoE schedule ownership and expert placement currently depend on the generated field that stores a routing. That couples logical router identity to storage and prevents distinct routers from sharing a field. This PR associates schedules and placement coordinates with `MoeRouterId`, and validates schedule use against the router that last populated the field.

## Why field identity is insufficient

A logical router represents one MoE routing operation; its routing field holds the resulting token-to-expert assignment. If two routers eventually share storage, they must retain separate schedules and placement identities.

Illustrative pseudocode for a stale schedule after reuse:

```text
route(router=0, output=shared)  // builds schedule_0
route(router=1, output=shared)  // builds schedule_1
matmul(routing=shared, schedule=schedule_0)
```

Previously, validation rejected the second producer of `shared` outright. Merely allowing repeated field names would leave the schedule check unable to distinguish the two owners: both refer to `shared`. The new checks allow distinct router IDs to populate the same field, but reject the final matmul because its schedule belongs to router 0 while the field contains router 1's routing.

## Carry logical ownership through lowering and emission

Loopy-to-Tron lowering now records router IDs against the original Loopy routing names, independently of the Tron fields those names resolve to. Expert weights retain that logical ID for placement, and `MoeScheduleInfo` records it as the schedule's owner.

C++ emission uses this ownership to select the schedules built by each routing operation and to enumerate that router's expert-weight tensors for placement. When a schedule's C++ type needs the expert count, emission follows its owner ID to the corresponding route statement and routing declaration.

Tron validation requires unique router IDs and walks statements in order, tracking the latest router to write each field. Each expert matmul must use a schedule owned by that router and declared for the same weight tensor.

This builds on routing-name resolution in [#4458](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4458). Lowering still creates one routing field per logical router here; later stack layers analyze reuse, materialize shared fields, and preserve runtime buffer capacity.

## Validation

The changed TronCheck cases accept distinct router IDs sharing a field and reject a schedule from the previous router after that field is refilled. Adapted cases cover matching schedule ownership, rejection of a different weight source, and duplicate router-ID rejection, including at the C++ emission boundary.

title: ingest: Compute reusable MoE routing assignments
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
MoE routing intermediates currently receive separate storage even when an earlier routing is no longer needed before a later one is built. This PR computes which routings can share a storage slot and when to prepare its synchronization channel, providing the plan that the next stack layer uses to share routing fields.

## Planning reusable routing slots

`RoutingAssignment` maps each routing intermediate to the first-written routing that owns its planned slot. The allocator processes routings in first-write order, so ownership follows execution order even when declarations appear in a different order.

For an illustrative example, suppose `routing_a` is written at statement 0 and last read at statement 1, while `routing_b` is written at statement 24. If both have eight experts, select two experts per token (`topK = 2`), and have compatible channel requirements, the plan maps both to `routing_a`. Preparation for `routing_b` is scheduled after `routing_a`'s last read and before `routing_b`'s write executes.

Routings use a separate slot pool within the existing buffer allocator. This reuses its lifetime checks, channel compatibility rules, and reuse-gap heuristic, which leaves separation between uses to limit additional waiting. Matching expert counts and `topK` values ensure that a shared slot can hold either routing. Overlapping lifetimes or incompatible requirements receive separate slots.

## Stack scope

The parent, [#4459](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4459), separates logical router identity from storage identity. This layer returns the routing assignment and applies its preparation schedule, while lowering still creates a distinct field and guard channel for each routing. Scheduled operations retain the original routing names and therefore resolve to those individual channels here. [#4461](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4461) consumes the assignment to materialize shared fields and channels.

## Validation

Analysis tests cover shared ownership independent of declaration order, exactly one preparation between successive routing lifetimes, and separate slots for overlapping lifetimes or mismatched expert counts and `topK` values.

title: ingest: Materialize shared MoE routing fields
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
The reuse analysis can assign compatible MoE routings to one storage slot, but LoopyTron currently discards that assignment and declares separate fields and guard channels. Apply the assignment during lowering so those routings share storage while retaining their distinct logical router identities.

## Materializing the shared slot

As an illustrative example, suppose the analysis assigns `routing_b` to the slot owned by `routing_a`, the earlier writer. Both routing names now resolve to one generated field. Each routing operation populates that field for its own consumers.

Lowering carries the assignment in `envRoutingAssignment`. It resolves each routing to its canonical owner, then uses `stateRoutingFieldByOwner` to find or create that owner's field. Each logical routing gets its own environment binding pointing to the shared field, and the field combines their source provenance.

The field is created on the first encounter of any slot member. This handles an alias declared before its owner: declaration order does not change the owner selected by the lifetime analysis.

Channel creation also reuses the shared field's existing guard channel. The preparation and read/write schedules already refer to logical Loopy names; resolving those names through their bindings now directs successive uses to the same channel, synchronizing access to the shared storage.

## Logical identity and stack scope

Each logical routing retains its own `RoutingEnvInfo` and `MoeRouterId`. Schedules and expert-weight placement continue to use that logical ID even when multiple bindings point to the same field.

Earlier stack entries supply the reuse analysis and separation of logical identity from storage. This PR materializes that plan. Generated code still reconstructs the routing object with `emplace` on each use; in-place rebuilding is a subsequent change.

## Validation

The added lowering tests check that compatible, separated routings produce one field owned by the earliest writer, including when the alias is declared first. Generated-C++ checks verify that only the owner field is declared, that the two-router fixture constructs two expert schedules, and that the weights retain distinct router IDs in their placement coordinates.

title: Remove redundant blocks around generated single-call statements
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body: Generated plugins wrap plain tensor visits and attention-preparation calls in unnecessary standalone blocks. Emit those calls directly: each is a single ordinary call with no local declarations or scope-dependent lifetime.

title: Remove redundant outer blocks from generated kernel methods
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Generated kernel and MoE blend methods wrap an already complete block in another block, adding an unnecessary brace pair and indentation level. Use a smart block constructor to remove that redundant wrapper while keeping the method builders responsible for ensuring braced bodies.

`Cpp.block` reuses a block when it is the sole child and wraps any other statement list in a block. This avoids relying on the scheduling strategies continuing to return `Block`, a requirement their `Statement` return types do not enforce. Blocks alongside other statements retain their scopes, preserving variable and tracing lifetimes.

title: Remove obsolete MoE kernel argument metadata
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
`KernelInfo.kernelMoeVars` describes extra MoE loop variables, but every constructor supplies an empty list and C++ generation never reads it. Its only explicit consumer is the Tron pretty-printer, which adds an empty `()` suffix to kernel headers. Remove this obsolete metadata and the suffix it produces.

MoE iteration is already represented by `kernelIterSpace`: `QBatchItemsExpertPairs` carries the routing name and expert-selection count used to generate expert-major loops. Removing `kernelMoeVars` from the IR, Loopy-to-Tron lowering, and example kernels therefore leaves generated kernel signatures and execution unchanged. This layer simplifies the Tron representation and its textual output; the preceding stack's C++ formatting changes are separate.

title: Remove obsolete expert-view initialization statements
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Loopy-to-Tron lowering emits `MoeExpertViewInitStmt` as though an expert view needs initialization after routing is built, but both C++ execution paths discard the statement. The view is already bound to its routing optional and model parameter by the generated state constructor. Remove this obsolete operation so the Tron IR and trace sidecar no longer describe initialization that does not execute.

An expert view provides routed access to expert-indexed parameters such as biases. Its constructor binds to the `std::optional` that holds routing, rather than to a particular routing value; each forward pass fills that same optional. The existing `ExpertViewInfo` declaration therefore supplies everything needed to generate the state field and constructor initializer.

Lowering now stops after resolving that declaration. Remove the unused statement variant and its provenance, pretty-printing, trace-sidecar, and C++ dispatch cases, and update the lowering documentation to describe constructor binding. Generated C++ execution is unchanged; textual Tron output and sidecar records lose the no-op initialization entry.

title: Render empty generated blocks compactly
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body: Empty generated C++ blocks currently contain line breaks and an indented blank line, adding noise to bodies such as the `plugin_batch` constructor and an inactive `patch_logits_in_place` method. Render `Block []` directly as `{}` so these empty bodies stay compact. Nonempty blocks retain their existing multiline formatting, and generated behavior is unchanged.

title: ingest: Give routing environment bindings a record
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
LoopyTron's routing binding stores the original Loopy variable and generated Tron routing-field name as positional arguments to `EnvInfo`. Adding metadata to that binding requires updating positional construction and pattern matches throughout lowering.

Group those values in a `RoutingEnvInfo` record and use named fields at construction and lookup sites. This is a representation-only refactor that prepares the binding to hold the logical router ID in the next PR; ID allocation and routing-field allocation keep their existing behavior.

title: ingest: Store router identity in its environment binding
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
LoopyTron stores each logical routing's generated field name in its environment binding, but keeps its `MoeRouterId` in a separate map keyed by the same Loopy name. Store the ID in `RoutingEnvInfo` alongside the variable and field name, removing the parallel map.

Declarations are lowered before the function body, so the ID starts as `Nothing`. Lowering `MoeRoute` assigns the next dense ID and updates the binding; `MoeMatmul` retrieves it for expert-weight placement and schedule ownership. This preserves numbering in statement order and the error when a routing's ID is missing.

The binding remains keyed by the logical Loopy routing name. That keeps router identity independent of the generated field used for storage, ready for the subsequent PR that lets multiple routings share a field.

title: Iterate generated MoE kernels over flat expert rows
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron

title: Expose read-only MoE routing row views
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
`moe_routing` exposes writable per-expert and flattened row containers, although both must agree with each other and with the cached active-expert IDs. Make the two containers private and expose read-only views, preventing callers from independently modifying either representation.

The routing API distinguishes the three kinds of access:

```cpp
routing.active_experts();        // Existing API: one ID per nonempty expert.
routing.rows_for(expert);        // This expert's (token, slot) tuples.
routing.rows_in_expert_order();  // Encoded token-slot IDs, grouped by expert ID.
```

`rows_for()` returns a span of const tuples indexed by `expert_row_id`; `rows_in_expert_order()` returns a span of const encoded IDs. Generated and handwritten activation loops, matmul preparation and readiness handling, and statistics use these accessors instead of accessing the vectors directly.

The views borrow the existing storage, preserving row element types, construction, allocations, and ordering. This establishes the access boundary separately from the following changes to row representation and storage.

title: Use encoded token-slot IDs for per-expert rows
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
`moe_routing` stores each routed row as a `(token, slot)` tuple in its per-expert vectors and as an encoded `token_slot_id` in its flat vector. Use encoded IDs in both, giving the two row views the same element type and allowing construction of the flat sequence to copy those IDs directly.

This changes `rows_for(expert)` from a view of const tuples to a view of const encoded IDs. Its current callers use only row counts and indices. Callers that need a tuple use `expert_row(expert, row)`, which now decodes the stored ID and preserves its existing tuple return value.

The per-expert vectors and flat vector remain separate, with the same row ordering and worker assignment. This isolates the row representation and accessor type change so the following storage-consolidation PR can preserve those accessor signatures.

title: Store MoE routing rows once
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Store `moe_routing`'s routed rows once, in a single vector partitioned by expert offsets, instead of in both per-expert vectors and a flattened copy. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

`moe_routing` kept every encoded token-slot row twice: in a vector for its expert, read through `rows_for(expert)`, and in a flat expert-ordered vector, read through `rows_in_expert_order()`. Both copies had to agree, and every expert needed its own inner vector.

## Layout

`reset()` now builds the rows with a counting sort. It counts each expert's rows, turns the counts into offsets with a prefix sum, then walks the batch in token and slot order, placing each row at its expert's next free position. That walk reproduces the order the per-expert vectors had, which matmuls, readiness waits, and worker assignment depend on.

For example, if experts 0, 1, and 2 receive rows `[A, B]`, `[]`, and `[C]`, where the letters stand for encoded token-slot IDs, the layout is:

```text
rows_:           [A, B, C]
expert_offsets_: [0, 2, 2, 3]
```

`rows_for(expert)` views `rows_` between that expert's adjacent offsets, so an empty expert is a repeated offset, and `rows_in_expert_order()` views the whole vector. Only `rows_` holds routed rows on the heap; the offsets live in a fixed array. Keeping offsets rather than cached spans lets a copied or moved routing object derive its views from its own `rows_`.

Accessor signatures, the active-expert list, and the per-expert counts reported in traces are unchanged. `rows_for()` wraps its slice with `as_indexed_span` from #4673.

## Validation

The precomputed-routing test now checks the exact per-expert and flattened row order, the active experts, and the preserved per-token indices for out-of-order batch tokens with two slots each, including empty experts. Its sections check a copied routing object after its source is destroyed, which catches views into the source's storage, and routing objects rebuilt in place with the same batch and with an empty batch, which catch state carried over from the previous build.

title: Evaluate Tron build recipes before the lab handoff
author: hvaneenoo-positron
body:
Build Tron could pass the lab-cache readiness check and still fail before compilation because evaluating its checkout flake needed a Haskell package plan outside the published build-input closure. PR #4476 exposed this after cache GC.

Evaluate the final C++ recipe in the existing Prepare Tron build inputs job after model plugin generation. Publish the derivation graph, realized build inputs (including the exact plugins), pinned CI Python, and test/benchmark environments as one handoff.

Wait for lab cache only checks availability of that complete closure. Build Tron acquires and roots it, then builds the named derivation outputs without evaluating the checkout flake. Existing required check names and runtime cache reuse are preserved. Compiler-dependency preparation and mirroring now start after plugin generation, trading their earlier overlap for one preparation stage.

Validation:

- The integration regression copies a signed publication into an isolated store, runs GC, and executes the real lab bootstrap/build steps with checkout-flake evaluation rejected and substitutes/remote builders disabled. It checks both runtime contents and retention through another GC. Restoring the evaluating workflow makes the test fail.

title: Remove redundant MoE row accessor
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Remove `moe_routing::expert_row()` so matmul views and readiness remapping use each expert's encoded row view directly. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

`rows_for(expert)` returns a view of that expert's encoded token-slot IDs. `expert_row(expert, row)` indexed the same view, then split the ID into a `(token, slot)` tuple, and the matmul input and output views immediately rebuilt a `token_slot_id` from that tuple to index activations and outputs.

The matmul views now capture the expert's row view and index activations and outputs with its IDs. Readiness remapping iterates the same view and reads `token()` and `slot()` only where the waitable layout needs the components. Row order and the batch-rank mapping are unchanged, and the tuple alias and `<tuple>` include go away with the accessor.

Note [MoeRouting Channel] now refers to half-rebuilt routing rows instead of the removed per-expert container.

title: Represent all-device placement with an explicit strategy
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
All-device placement is currently encoded as a null strategy: `all_devices()` returns `nullptr`, and placement wrappers interpret a missing base as an instruction to use every device. Make that policy an explicit `AllDevices` strategy so wrappers can delegate through a uniform, non-null interface.

For example, an expert-placement wrapper handles expert weights itself and delegates ordinary weights to its base. With the default policy, it currently needs a separate null-base path to reset placement to all devices. An explicit `AllDevices` base performs that reset through the normal delegation path, selecting all available devices permitted by the active mask.

Model selection now supplies this default whenever no specialized strategy is selected. Installing a strategy or constructing a router/expert wrapper requires a non-null strategy; callers that want default placement pass `all_devices()`. This establishes the non-null contract used by the subsequent strategy-ownership refactor.

The existing expert-placement test now uses the explicit default base. It seeds a prior single-device placement, then verifies that an ordinary tensor is placed on both devices in a sparse active mask. This checks that delegation restores the default device set rather than retaining the previous selection.

title: Report tensor placement once per load scope
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
With `TRON_LOG_PLACEMENT` enabled, a composed placement strategy emits multiple reports for one model load. Report placement once when the load scope ends, so the output corresponds to the load rather than the number of strategy objects.

Each `PlacementStrategy` destructor currently prints and clears the same shared tensor/device counters. For example, destroying an expert-placement wrapper around `AllDevices` produces the populated report followed by `Tensor device counts: null`: the first destructor has already cleared the records before the second runs.

Move reporting and record cleanup into `log_placement()`, called by the existing `with_placement_strategy` scope before it destroys the strategy chain. Make the individual strategy destructor defaulted. The scope already encloses model loading, so it provides a single place to emit the accumulated report and clear the counters and current tensor name.

title: Own tensor placement through a load-scoped context
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Tensor placement currently spreads ownership and operations across a global strategy pointer, two scope helpers, and a free function. It also silently chooses all masked devices when no strategy is installed. This PR introduces a scope-owned `placement_context` that groups those operations and requires an explicit policy for hardware placement, while keeping standalone CPU tensor loads independent of placement.

## Put ownership and placement operations in one context

`with_placement_strategy` already provided an RAII lifetime, but it moved the strategy into a global owning pointer. `placement_context` instead owns the strategy directly; the global pointer only borrows the active context. Construction installs the context, and destruction reports placement, clears the pointer, and destroys the owned strategy.

The context also replaces the two separate placement entry points:

- `begin_tensor(request)` replaces constructing `with_placement`, whose constructor began a logical tensor but had no corresponding exit operation.
- `next_tile_devices()` replaces `place_on_devices()`, delegating to the strategy and retaining the central device validation and placement recording.

For example, a standalone hardware caller explicitly chooses a policy before allocating tiles:

```cpp
placement_context context(all_devices());
context.begin_tensor(tensor_placement_request::ordinary_tensor("weight"));
// Hardware tile allocations use current_placement_context().next_tile_devices().
```

Model loading installs its selected strategy through the same context. Standalone hardware helpers and tests that previously relied on the fallback now explicitly select `all_devices()`.

## Require a context at the hardware boundary

`current_placement_context()` asserts if no context is installed. Hardware allocation and mock placement use this required accessor.

The real safetensors loader supports both host and hardware tensors, so it uses `try_current_placement_context()` and begins a request only when a context exists. A standalone CPU load therefore needs no placement policy. During a model load, all tensor requests still reach the installed context, including host tensors and missing optional tensors, preserving the request sequence used by shuffled placement.

This retains the existing non-reentrant, globally accessible scope. Placement algorithms are unchanged, and logging state remains global for the following PR to address.

## Validation

The placement test checks policy selection across separate all-device and rotating scopes on a sparse device mask, and verifies that required context lookup aborts both before and after those scopes. The safetensors fixture test now loads a CPU tensor without a context and checks all 100 values.

title: Remove unused shuffled placement state
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Shuffled placement retains bookkeeping it never uses and keeps its random generator alive after construction. Remove the unused `total_tensors` and `placed_tensors` fields, the empty destructor, and the now-unneeded `<atomic>` include.

Make the random generator local to the constructor, where it creates the shuffled tensor-rank list. Its seed, shuffle operation, rank consumption, and placement sequence are unchanged.

title: Remove partial locking from serial placement
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Shuffled placement locks its tensor-rank list, but the shared device-mask table and tile cursor remain unsynchronized. Placement runs serially during model loading, so this lock does not establish a supported concurrent operation and obscures the actual contract.

Remove the rank-list mutex and its lock guard. Rank consumption, tile rotation, and seeded shuffle order are unchanged. This cleanup does not add concurrent placement support.

title: Keep placement reports within their loading context
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
`placement_context` already controls when a placement report is written, but the current tensor name and per-device counts still live in process-global variables that must be cleared between loads. Move that state into the context so the report data has the same owner and lifetime as the loading operation it describes.

When a context is constructed with `TRON_LOG_PLACEMENT` set, it creates a private `placement_log`. `begin_tensor()` records the tensor name, and `next_tile_devices()` counts tile placements on each selected device. Context destruction writes the existing JSON report and releases the log, replacing manual clearing of shared state. With logging disabled, no log is allocated. The environment setting is now checked when each context is constructed rather than during static initialization.

The log implementation stays in the source file, keeping its maps and report formatting out of the public header. This changes ownership of report state; the preceding PR already establishes explicit placement scopes and their reporting boundary.

title: Pass device sets explicitly to placement policies and allocation
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Placement policies currently consult the ambient device mask at different times: some capture it during construction, others read it for each tensor or tile. Hardware weight loading narrows that mask to v2 devices after tensor placement has already begun. Give policies an explicit device set and give allocation an explicit eligibility mask, so those two decisions no longer depend on when a policy happens to read global state.

## Explicit policy and allocation inputs

Each policy factory receives the devices it may use. Rotated, shuffled, all-device, router, and expert placement retain that set for their lifetime. The model loader computes the set once from the selected devices and v2-capable hardware, and uses it consistently when choosing and composing policies.

Hardware weight loading separately passes its supported device mask into allocation. The context intersects the policy's selection with that mask, rejects an empty result, and logs the devices actually selected. Quantization no longer temporarily changes `current_device_mask`. Standalone hardware callers explicitly construct an all-device policy over their selected v2-capable devices and use the same allocation eligibility check.

For example, a router policy constructed for devices `{1, 3}` selects those devices even if an unrelated ambient mask contains only device 0. If a particular allocation supports only device 3, its final placement is `{3}`. Normal model loading constructs policies over the supported set from the outset.

## Validation

The existing router/rotation case now uses sparse explicit devices and an unrelated ambient mask, checks a narrower allocation mask, and verifies that router placement still does not advance ordinary rotation. Expert-placement cases pass their device sets directly, preserving coverage of restricted devices, replica counts, delegation, and rotation.

This changes device inputs at policy construction and allocation boundaries. The existing context lookup and tensor-loading interfaces remain in place.

title: Rename placement strategy start_placing to begin_tensor
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body: Rename `PlacementStrategy::start_placing` to `begin_tensor` to describe beginning placement for one logical tensor. Update overrides, callers, and comments without changing behavior. This establishes the name before the strategy-ownership and placement-context refactors.

title: Keep expert overrides from advancing base placement rotation
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
TL;DR for reviewers: this change does not meaningfully change anything, it only refactors the `ExpertsByPlan` strategy to be shaped like the others so they can all be improved uniformly by later PRs in the stack. There was no good reason `ExpertsByPlan` did not already behave like this. I recommend rubber-stamping :) 

---

Expert tiles placed by a load-aware plan currently advance the wrapped strategy's ordinary-tensor rotation, even though that strategy did not choose their devices. Preserve the base cursor across expert overrides so ordinary placement resumes where it left off.

For example, with four devices and one replica, ordinary tiles select devices 0 and 1. An expert tile then uses device 0 according to its expert plan. Previously, the next ordinary tile selected device 3; it now selects device 2. The expert's own placement is unchanged.

`ExpertsByPlan` saves the shared cursor on the first expert request, retains it across consecutive expert requests, and restores it before delegating the next ordinary tensor to the base strategy. Expert allocations can advance the shared object's temporary cursor without affecting the saved base position.

The existing rotation test now checks this sequence and expects ordinary placement to resume at device 2. This separates the policy change from the subsequent strategy-ownership refactor, which removes the shared-cursor save/restore machinery while retaining the behavior established here.

title: Disable wait statistics by default
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
Timed waits update two atomic counters shared by all threads, although only diagnostic tests read them. Those updates add contention during inference. This PR makes them optional with `TRON_MWAIT_STATS`, defaulting to **OFF**. `-DTRON_MWAIT_STATS=ON` restores the counters and their test assertions. The wait mechanisms and timeout logic stay the same.

FPGA CI runs both settings in one CMake build. Diagnostic tests share the existing libraries and add three compiled objects: the instrumented wait implementation and two test sources. Each executable links exactly one wait implementation. Coverage enables counters; inference benchmarks leave them off.

At previous head `57bf6cf3`, the additional diagnostic targets took **4.8 seconds on four Andoria-11 CPU cores**, with compiler caching disabled. That covers three compilations and two links; all 201 existing objects remained unchanged. It measures the added targets, not total CI time.

| 1 | 286.31 → 318.53 (+11.25%) | 207.59 → 223.49 (+7.66%) |
| 4 | 183.95 → 196.71 (+6.94%) | 421.10 → 438.54 (+4.14%) |

Values are medians of four process results per setting, with one warmup and three measured iterations. Run order alternated, and all eight paired throughput comparisons improved. title: Extract cyclic replica mask calculation
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
Rotating and shuffled placement duplicate the calculation used to fill their cyclic device-mask tables. Extract that calculation into `cyclic_replica_mask` and call it from both table-building loops, preserving the existing placement sequence.

For table entry `i`, the old loops selected device positions `i * replicas` through `i * replicas + replicas - 1`, wrapping through the supplied device set. The helper computes those same positions directly. The tables, cursor preservation, and shuffled starting ranks remain unchanged.

The subsequent [strategy-ownership PR](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4198) reuses this helper to select each tile's devices directly and removes the tables.

title: Represent attention K and V placement roles
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Add distinct C++ placement roles for attention key and value projections so placement policies can identify them without inspecting tensor names.

## Role representation

Placement requests currently distinguish ordinary tensors, MoE routers, and expert weights. Extend that classification with `attention_key_projection_tensor` and `attention_value_projection_tensor`, following the existing pattern of variant alternatives, named request constructors, and role predicates.

This PR supplies the C++ representation. Subsequent PRs preserve ingest's existing K/V semantics in generated placement requests, then use those roles to place K and V on separate device groups. Generated requests and device placement remain unchanged at this layer.

title: Preserve attention K and V roles in generated placement requests
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Preserve attention K and V semantics in generated placement requests so C++ placement policies can distinguish the two projections.

## Preserve the existing classification

Ingest already recognizes checkpoint keys such as `model.layers.11.self_attn.k_proj.weight` as `WeightK`. When declaring these weights during Loopy-to-Tron lowering, however, both roles fall through to `OrdinaryTensor`, so generated visitors lose the distinction for placement.

Carry `WeightK` and `WeightV` into distinct Tron placement kinds, then emit the corresponding `attention_key_projection_tensor(...)` and `attention_value_projection_tensor(...)` requests in the generated tensor visitor. This uses the existing semantic annotations; C++ does not need to reinterpret checkpoint names. Q remains an ordinary placement request.

The preceding PR supplies the C++ request constructors. Existing placement policies handle these new roles through their ordinary paths, so device placement is unchanged here. The following PR uses the distinction to place K and V on separate device groups.

## Validation

Extend the existing placement-classification test with explicitly annotated weights named `key_matrix`, `value_matrix`, and `query_matrix`. It checks that K and V retain distinct placement kinds and emit their corresponding C++ requests, while Q remains ordinary, demonstrating that propagation follows the semantic annotations rather than the tensor names.

title: ingest: recognize nested language-model weight semantics
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Recognize nested text-model projection weights so ingestion assigns their semantic roles and layer numbers for Muse Glimmer, Gemma 3, and Gemma 4.

`guessWeightSemantics` only matched weights under `model.layers.*`, but these models put their text layers under `model.language_model.layers.*`. For example, `model.language_model.layers.10.self_attn.k_proj.weight` returned `Nothing`; it now returns `Just (Weight WeightK, 10)`. These weight tags also seed activation semantics used by intermediate logging.

The classifier now matches the original checkpoint key against either supported text-layer namespace, sharing the existing attention and MLP projection rules. Matching is explicit because semantic tags contain a role and layer number but no component identity: classifying vision projections the same way would lose the distinction between text and vision layers. Vision namespaces therefore remain unclassified.

## Validation

The regression test checks Muse Glimmer K/V classification and layer identity; it fails on the parent revision because the K projection is unclassified. Additional cases check the existing `model.layers.*` format and reject vision-prefixed projections and projection biases.

title: Remove unused fallback tensor_latch instance interface
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Remove unused fallback `tensor_latch` state and methods to clarify that the channel backing owns synchronization.
This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

Fallback channels wait for all producers through a latch owned by `channel_fallback_latch_backing`. The default `tensor_latch` selects that backing but is never instantiated by it, leaving its own latch field and runtime methods unused.

Remove that unused instance interface and retain the backing alias and static metadata. The accompanying comment now identifies the backing as the owner of the whole-phase latch.

title: Select channel storage by the latch's readiness scope
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Select channel storage from each latch's readiness scope so latches no longer depend on concrete channel backing types. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

## Readiness and storage selection

Each `tensor_latch` previously selected its channel storage through a `backing` template alias. This required `threading.hpp` to forward-declare backing types implemented alongside `channel` in `models/common.hpp`. Each latch also declared an unused `is_fallback` flag, duplicating the classification supplied by its backing.

A latch now declares a `readiness_scope` describing when its results become readable:

- `whole_phase`: all items become readable after every producer finishes the phase. The channel uses one shared countdown latch.
- `per_item`: items can become readable independently. The channel stores one tensor latch per item; that latch retains its existing payload-based, explicitly signaled, or tile-level readiness mechanism.

The channel selects a `channel_backing` specialization from that scope at compile time. This puts storage selection alongside the channel while letting latches describe readiness without naming channel implementation types. The backing methods and synchronization operations are unchanged.

title: Remove the signaled latch's unused copy operations
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Remove unused copy and assignment operations from the signaled tensor latch so its supported operations match how channels manage readiness words. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

A signaled latch owns an atomic readiness word that a producer publishes after writing an item. Channel backings store these latches in an `indexed_vector`, whose sizing operation requires move construction but does not use copy construction or either assignment operator.

Keep the `noexcept` move constructor for vector sizing before producers or consumers can observe the readiness words. Remove the unused copy constructor, copy assignment, and move assignment, making accidental copies or assignments fail to compile instead of duplicating or overwriting readiness state.

title: Remove unused channel, barrier and wait code
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Remove unused channel, barrier, and wait helpers so the synchronization interfaces reflect the operations their callers actually use. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

The channel callback factory and latch polling wrapper have no callers. The barrier move constructor is also unused and incompletely preserves the metadata needed by a later `reset`; removing it avoids retaining an unsupported move operation.

The low-level wait cleanup removes unused convenience overloads: callers already append explicit `readiness_source` objects, which distinguish raw payload markers from atomic readiness words, and use the remaining polling operations. With the raw-pointer append overload gone, the shared append implementation becomes the sole public overload. Waitable views also drop their unused timeout argument: existing callers wait without a timeout, and the old argument applied separately to each entry rather than bounding the entire wait.

For MoE, remove the unused `whole_phase_activation_ready` tag and its launcher overload. Whole-phase readiness remains supported by the existing remapping path, which passes a single readiness entry through unchanged because every expert row waits on that same source.

title: Keep the producer count in the whole-phase backing
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Move the stored producer count from `channel` into its whole-phase backing so readiness-specific state lives with the implementation that uses it. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

A whole-phase backing makes the buffer readable after every producer finishes. It therefore needs the producer count to re-arm its completion latch at the start of each phase. Previously, `channel` retained that count and passed it to every `backing.prepare` call, although the per-item backing ignored it.

The whole-phase backing now saves the count during `reset`, where it already receives it, and uses that saved value in an argument-free `prepare()`. The per-item backing adopts the same signature, allowing the channel to prepare either backing without retaining an extra count. The channel still configures its participant barriers during reset, and the readiness latch is re-armed at the same point in the phase transition.

title: Correct channel reading and producer-completion docs
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Correct the channel synchronization documentation and remove a redundant attention query lookup so callers can see where reads wait and how producers complete a phase. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

Fallback channels track readiness for an entire phase: `start_reading` waits until every producer has called `finish_writing`, while `start_reading_at` only returns the requested item. The previous documentation placed the fallback wait in `start_reading_at`. The corrected explanation distinguishes this from per-index channels, which wait for individual items, and makes the ordering constraint explicit: a thread that producers depend on must not enter the fallback read wait before those producers finish.

Attention query channels are statically required to use fallback latches, so their existing `start_reading` already waits for all queries. Remove the following `start_reading_at(0)`, whose result was discarded, and update the attention and RoPE comments to describe the actual wait.

The producer-completion documentation also now describes logical participants rather than requiring completion on the thread that started writing. Each participant must call `finish_writing` once per phase, possibly from a matmul completion callback, because the next `prepare` waits for all configured producers.

title: Replace channel fallback flags with readiness-scope checks
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Replace `channel::is_fallback` with `channel::scope` so attention and feed-forward callers state their readiness requirements directly. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

The parent PR introduces `readiness_scope` and uses it to select channel storage. This layer exposes that same scope to callers instead of reducing it to a fallback flag: `whole_phase` means all items become readable after every producer finishes, while `per_item` allows individual items to become readable independently.

## Caller requirements

Attention already requires whole-phase readiness for its query and output channels. Its compile-time assertions now express that requirement directly.

The asynchronous dense W2 launch starts before the main thread runs `activate_and_multiply`. At that point, calling `start_reading` on a whole-phase activation channel would wait for producer work that the same thread has yet to perform. A per-item channel only waits for phase preparation; the matmul's waitable handles data readiness separately.

Previously, this call was guarded by a negated fallback check. However, the dense activation channel is always a signaled, per-item channel, so the branch that skipped `start_reading` was unreachable. Replace the conditional with a compile-time assertion requiring `per_item`, then call `start_reading` unconditionally. This preserves the existing execution order and makes an incompatible future channel change fail at compile time.

## Validation

The existing channel classification test now checks the explicit scopes: fallback producers use whole-phase readiness, while signaled and block producers use per-item readiness.

title: rinzler: take strftime_now's local offset from libc
author: jw-pos
body:
`strftime_now` resolved local time through `chrono::Local`, while C++ callers and the crate's parity oracle use `localtime_r`. The two look for zoneinfo in different places. Under the Nix toolchain, glibc cannot find the zone named by `TZ` and falls back to UTC, while chrono finds it in `/usr/share/zoneinfo`. With `TZ=America/Los_Angeles` the epoch-pinned tool-call example then renders 1969-12-31 while `t_rinzler_request` expects 1970-01-01. `strftime_now_matches_c_strftime_for_served_formats` fails the same way.

This change takes the UTC offset from `localtime_r` and formats with chrono, so the rendered date always agrees with the C library. `libc` moves from a dev-dependency to a dependency at the same pinned version; `Cargo.lock` is unchanged.

Validation (Nix toolchain, andoria-08):
- `cargo test` in `rust/minijinja`: 40/40 under `TZ=America/Los_Angeles`, `UTC` and `Pacific/Kiritimati`; before the change the parity test fails under Los Angeles.
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` clean.
- With the change applied to a full native build: `t_rinzler_request` (383/383) and `t_minijinja_rs` pass under `TZ=America/Los_Angeles`; both fail without it.

The existing `t_minijinja_rs` and `t_rinzler_request` cases already cover the behavior, so no test is added.

title: slice: limit host-test memory per NUMA node
author: hvaneenoo-positron
body:
Fixes #4593.

## Problem

Tron binds an instance whose slots share one NUMA node strictly to that node. `numa_alloc_policy()` in `src/system/system.cpp` uses `HWLOC_MEMBIND_BIND | HWLOC_MEMBIND_STRICT`, so the instance's anonymous (non-file, non-hugepage) memory cannot spill to the other node.

Slice admitted launches against one system-wide budget, `MemTotal − hugepages − 2 GB`, on the assumption that allocations spill across nodes. On andoria-02/14 (377 GiB, 140 × 1 GiB hugepages per node), that is about 95 GiB for the whole box but only about 47 GiB per node. Slice could therefore put `t_generate_host_2-slow` and `t_generate_host_2-fast` (about 40 GB) on node 0 together. The kernel OOM-killed `-fast` (`CONSTRAINT_MEMORY_POLICY, nodemask=0`), and the runner unit's `OOMPolicy=stop` stopped the GitHub runner and cancelled the job. 29 Test host jobs failed this way from 15-Sep to 24-Sep, including merge-queue runs. The data is in #4593.

## Change

- `bin/slice`: new `MemoryBudget` and `get_node_budgets_mb()`. Slice keeps the system budget and adds one budget per NUMA node, read from `/sys/devices/system/node`: node `MemTotal` minus node hugepages minus a share of the 2 GB safety margin.
  - A launch whose slots share one node is charged to that node and to the system.
  - A launch that spans nodes runs unbound, matching tron's `SYSTEM_NUMA_ALL` case, and is charged to the system only.
  - The run loop takes the first free aligned block whose node has room, so a heavy test moves to the other node instead of being OOM-killed.
  - A test that is alone on the box, or alone on its node, is still admitted, so the queue cannot deadlock.
  - Without NUMA data, or with the gate disabled, behavior is unchanged.
- `doc/slice.md`: the Out of memory section now describes both budgets and why the per-node one is needed.
- The bench path is unchanged. It already runs at most one test per NUMA node at a time.

## Tests

`bin/slice-tests/test_memory_budget.py` adds 8 tests:

- `test_run_moves_heavy_host_test_off_full_node` replays the andoria-14 placement through `cmd_run`: `-slow` at slot 0 and `-fast` hinted at slot 2. It fails on main (`-fast` launches at `--instance 2,8` on node 0 while `-slow` runs at `--instance 0,8`) and passes with this change.
- Unit tests cover:
  - per-node hugepage subtraction with unequal nodes
  - blocking when a node is full, using andoria-14's real numbers
  - releasing a node's charge
  - admitting a test that is alone on its node
  - multi-node launches checked against the system budget only
  - the system budget with and without NUMA data
  - no NUMA directories in `/sys`

```
nix develop --accept-flake-config .#slice-tests --command python3 -m pytest -q bin/slice-tests
743 passed
```

This has not been run on hardware. cloud-atlas-873f has the same memory layout as andoria-02/14 (377 GiB, 140 hugepages per node) if a live check is wanted.

title: Add a named ingest CI toolchain for Test ingest
author: hvaneenoo-positron
body:
## Summary

GCP's `Test ingest` job entered the full developer ingest shell (`.#ingest`), which brings GHC, cabal, haskell-language-server, fourmolu, and Haskell documentation components. The job only runs Python against the prebuilt ingest executable passed with `--ingest-bin`, so it uses none of them.

- Add `ingestCiToolchainDeps` (the ingest Python environment, `gnumake`, `git`) and `devShells.ingest-ci`.
- Switch `Test ingest`'s "Prepare ingest environment" step to `nix develop .#ingest-ci`.
- Move the shared Python shell setup (`PYTHONPATH`, `TRON_INGEST_LIBSTDCXX_PATH`) into `ingestPythonShellEnv`, used by both `mkIngestShell` and the new shell.

`.#ingest` and `.#ingest-cuda` are unchanged for developers.

## Why

This prepares for pinning the latest main build in the Nix binary caches: the pinned set should name the toolchains CI actually uses rather than everything a developer shell pulls in. The developer-only inputs of `.#ingest` add about 1.65 GiB on the regional cache that `Test ingest` never touches.

## Validation

- `.#ingest` and `.#ingest-cuda` evaluate to identical derivations before and after (`9n3xqm6z…-nix-shell.drv`, `wp9wi8xc…-nix-shell.drv`).
- `nix develop .#ingest-ci --ignore-environment` (keeping `HOME`, `CI`, `USER`, `LOGNAME`): `ghc`, `cabal`, `haskell-language-server`, `fourmolu`, `clang`, `gcc` absent; `git`, `make`, `python3` from the Nix store; `make test-ingest-python` → 368 passed; `ingest/build-model.py --help` runs.
- `nixfmt --check flake.nix`, `bin/ci/run-lint-checks.sh`, and `checks.x86_64-linux.ci-machinery-contracts` pass.
- The model pipeline smoke and logit steps need the builders' weights; this PR's `Test ingest` run is their validation.

No new test: `Test ingest` is a required check that runs every step inside this shell, so a missing tool fails it directly.

title: Attention path stats: AVX / AMX / FPGA shares and timers behind TRON_ATTN_STATS
author: jhan-positron
body:
## Short version

This PR counts how much of a model's attention work ran on each path (AVX, AMX, FPGA), and how long attention took, per layer and per pool worker (one thread of the application thread pool). 

One environment variable, `TRON_ATTN_STATS=1`, turns on the collection at run time. The numbers come out as FUSE leaves under `/model/<id>/attention/`, and as stderr summary at the end of a runtron run.

Perf impacts are neglectable. 

## Not in this PR
MoE models are not specifically scoped, it is likely MoE stats are not covered. Will add when AMX feature extends to MoE.

## Words used here

- visit: one call of `apply_page_tok`. That is one (query token, KV page of 64 tokens, KV head) triple that passed the page-level checks of `apply_page_range`. The AMX kernel serves a whole dense page per visit. The AVX loop serves the relevant K tokens of the page. An empty visit found no software work.
- forward: one model run for all users' pending token jobs. Forward class: `decode_like` when every token job has a listener (one generated token per user, but also a one-token final prompt chunk or a speculative verify step). `prompt_or_mixed` is every other forward. Under continuous batching (rinzler, the production server, adds and removes users between forwards) a forward that carries any user's prompt chunk is `prompt_or_mixed`. So `decode_like` counts pure-decode forwards only.
- listener: the consumer of one token job's logits. Every generated token has one, and so does the last token of a prompt chunk (the slice of a prompt that one forward processes). A prompt token without a listener only stores its K and V.
- pool worker: one thread of the application thread pool (`n_workers` in `summary`, 27 in the runs below). The attention workers of a forward are its last `n_attn_workers` pool workers. The first pool workers, the main helpers, do the non-attention work, and their attention rows read zero.

**Timers**, all in TSC cycles (`summary` carries `tsc_hz`):
- T1 = wall time of one model forward, taken by `forward_scope` (the one object that owns the per-forward record) inside `model::state::forward`, from just after the trace marker at its top to its return. The layers, the logits, the listener delivery and the release of the forward's synchronization latches (the latch arena) are inside. Scheduler work before and after is outside.
- T2 = busy time of one attention job on one worker. This is `attn_elapsed`, which exists today: both passes and the join, without the upstream K/V wait.
- T3 = wall time of one attention job as attention worker 0 sees it (entry to return), filed per layer. The layer and totals leaves carry the T3 and T4 keys (`wall_cycles_w0`, `period_cycles_w0` and their companions). The worker leaves do not.
- T4 = layer period on attention worker 0, filed per layer: from its first job of one attention operation to its first job of the next operation. The second minibatch of the same operation starts no period. The last layer of a forward has no period.
- T5 = `join_wait_cycles`: the time a worker spends waiting in the join with no join progress, in both join modes. In a hardware join it is the wait loop that ends when an FPGA pass or the other workers' software partials become ready. In a software-only join (CPU attention) it is the stretches of failed polls on the other workers' sections. T5 is inside T2.

## Doc and tests
Docs: `README.stats.md` describes the leaves and the switch.

Tests:

- New `t/t_attn_stats.cpp`, 17 cases. They cover tallies, rows, path sets, timers, class routing, the `forward_scope` object, the three job counts of a forward, the rows keyed by pool worker, the fold over the attention rows only, JSON leaves and their size, the leaves with the switch off, the exit report, FUSE registration with the weak_ptr rule, the last-wins takeover, and the EAGLE directory. A fork-based negative case checks that an out-of-range worker, layer or token job aborts (every hook index is a `TRON_ASSERT`). The switch rule (exactly "1") has no unit case: the reader is one function that reads the environment once, and the `TRON_ATTN_STATS=yes` runs on delphi-3bda and in the development container check the warning. The file is compiled into the `t_llama_unit` binary, so it needs no cost-data row of its own (a row needs a whole-host bench run).
- `t/t_llama_unit.cpp`: the fake-lane `apply_page_range` case asserts the stats-on tallies (32 AVX visits of 32 K tokens each, no AMX, no empty visit). The CI lane compiles without `TRON_AMX_DISPATCH`, and this case exercises the per-visit hook there. The case also reads the forward's path sets back (32 jobs `avx`, 32 jobs `none`) and checks that the visits land in the last pool row. It then repeats the call under a 2-worker split, where the same attention worker lands one row earlier. The two direct `stream_hw_joins` cases pass a real T5 accumulator and check 0. Every sweep there makes progress, so no wait is counted. After a production `apply_page_range` call, the state's own stats object is checked to follow `TRON_ATTN_STATS`.
- `t/t_amx_dispatch_dtype.cpp` asserts the amx/avx split against the kernel fakes' call counts. One section makes the fake `available()` answer false (one AVX visit that scored the whole page). After each call the path sets are read back (the AMX set exactly when the kernels ran, else the AVX set). The file also gets the `apply_page_range` argument main's copy lacks (the batch query mask). Main's copy does not compile with `-DTRON_AMX_DISPATCH=ON`, and #4557 carries the same fix.
- `t/heterogeneous_scheduler_compile.cpp`: the mixed-attention section checks the hardware join's T5 (greater than 0 and at most the join's wall time). The Q-reuse section reads T2, T3 and T4 back through `run_attention_job` (T3 includes the upstream K/V wait that a 20 ms probe makes real, T2 does not, so T3 exceeds T2). One section runs `run_joins` with no hardware plan against a producer that finishes 20 ms late, in three arms. Late producer with stats on: T5 greater than 0 and at most the wall time. Sections already done: T5 = 0. Stats flag off: T5 = 0. One section reaches `note_fpga_pass` through `prepare_hw_attention`. One case drives `model::state::forward` with the switch forced on and reads one whole record back (the class, the three job counts, T1 and the split) for a decode-like and a prompt-or-mixed forward. The fixtures that drive `apply_page_range` or `run_attention_job` with the switch on open a `forward_scope` first, as production does. This file and the direct `t_llama_unit` callers follow the `run_joins` and `stream_hw_joins` parameters.
- New `t/assertion_signal.hpp`: the fork-based helper that expects an abort, shared by `t_llama_unit.cpp`, `t_compute_attention_unit.cpp` and the negative case above (the first two had private copies).


## Why one environment variable and no CMake option

With the variable unset, a visit pays one test of a stack bool. The other hooks cost the same kind of test: three per attention job, one per failed poll and one per joined KV head in the software-only join, three per forward in `forward_scope`, and one per forward for the split. With the variable unset no hook writes memory or reads rdtsc. A visit costs est. 5,800 to 11,200 cycles (2.1 to 2.9 us per visit measured on 2026-09-01 at prompts 256 to 2048). The margin below a 1 % TPS change is therefore 60x to 400x. The A/A below is the check. 

## Off-state cost (A/A) and on-state cost

Setup: delphi-3bda, half of machine (socket 1, cards 90/93), runtron, CPU attention (`USE_HW_ATTN=0`). CPU attention is the worst case for the per-visit hooks, because every page visit is software. Model qwen-3-4b tp2, 8 users, 256 generated tokens, 3 interleaved repetitions per arm and cell. Arms: base and base2 = main 66c7bb8db1 with the variable unset (the same-binary pair gives the band). head = this branch at 9b3832eb4b with the variable unset. headon = the same binary with `TRON_ATTN_STATS=1`. TPS is the mean over the repetitions, with the sample sd. The band per cell was fixed before the runs: the largest of |base2 - base|, twice the largest per-arm sd, and 0.5 % of base.

| Cell | Arm | TPS | sd | vs base | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| prompt 1024 | base | 79.95 | 0.29 | | reference |
| prompt 1024 | base2 | 79.67 | 0.29 | -0.34 % | same binary: band 0.59 TPS (0.73 %) |
| prompt 1024 | head (switch unset) | 79.81 | 0.17 | -0.17 % | inside the band |
| prompt 1024 | headon (switch set) | 79.91 | 0.24 | -0.05 % | on-state cost: none visible |
| prompt 8192 | base | 17.12 | 0.00 | | reference |
| prompt 8192 | base2 | 17.11 | 0.02 | -0.10 % | same binary: band 0.09 TPS (the 0.5 % floor) |
| prompt 8192 | head (switch unset) | 17.25 | 0.04 | +0.77 % | faster than main, outside the band on the fast side (code placement, the same size of effect the PR 4587 measurement showed on this host) |
| prompt 8192 | headon (switch set) | 17.24 | 0.02 | +0.70 % | on-state cost: none visible |

TTFT (prefill time, max over the users), base / head / headon / base2: prompt 1024 3.146 / 3.153 / 3.161 / 3.147 s. Prompt 8192 52.65 / 52.78 / 53.01 / 52.68 s. The head with the switch set costs +0.4 % and +0.7 % of prefill time at the two prompt lengths (est. from single runs with sd 0.1 to 0.4 s: inside the run-to-run spread at 8192, at the edge at 1024).

Reading: the hooks with the variable unset cost nothing this A/A can see. The A/A resolves about 0.5 to 0.7 %. With the variable set, the counting costs nothing visible either. The pre-registered rule flips the switch to a build option only on a loss beyond the band at both cells. The environment variable stays.

Confirmation round on cbf1bb6c0c, the same cell at prompt 1024, three interleaved repetitions per arm, run after the main round on the same host:

| Arm | TPS | sd | vs base3 | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base3 (main, variable unset) | 79.78 | 0.41 | | reference of this round |
| head2 (cbf1bb6c0c, variable unset) | 79.81 | 0.38 | +0.04 % | inside the band |
| headon2 (cbf1bb6c0c, `TRON_ATTN_STATS=1`) | 80.10 | 0.17 | +0.39 % | on-state cost: none visible |

The A/A binaries are 9b3832eb4b and cbf1bb6c0c of this branch, both of 2026-09-24. The binary comparison under Cross-checks is of 04da001cb5, on 2026-09-30.

## Cross-checks

- Binary comparison (`objdump` of two runtron binaries, main 66c7bb8db1 and this branch at 04da001cb5, `exec/attnstats-20260930-objdump/objdump-check.sh`, 2026-09-30): 384 `apply_page_range` instantiations in both. The largest instantiation grows from 11,866 to 12,708 bytes (2,055 to 2,217 instructions). Lock-prefixed instructions: 0 in both. rdtsc in `apply_page_range`: 0 in both. The largest `run_attention_job` instantiation grows from 4,281 to 4,941 bytes and from 8 to 9 rdtsc reads. The added read runs only with the switch on. All `apply_page_range` code grows by 79,633 bytes over the 384 instantiations (+6.5 %). That is the switch-on code, compiled into every instantiation.
- The exit report prints only with the switch set: 0 `[attn-stats]` lines in every run with the variable unset, and the full report in every run with `TRON_ATTN_STATS=1`.
- Counter sanity against the closed-form visit model (the 2026-09-29 run below: qwen-3-4b tp2, 8 users, prompt 1024, 255 decode forwards, 36 layers, 8 KV heads). `ready_amx_visits` = 10,278,144, which equals the sum over the 255 steps of floor((1023 + t) / 64) x 36 x 8 x 8 exactly. `pending_amx_visits` = 6,912 = 3 steps x 2,304: the three steps whose new page was full took AMX in the same forward. That closes open point 11.1 of the design page. Prefill: `ready_amx_visits` 16,515,072 and `pending_avx_full_page_visits` 1,216,512. Full pages written in the current chunk take AVX even with AMX on, because the query sees them through several mask ranges. Token jobs by path set: decode 2,016 `avx+amx` and 24 `amx`. Prefill 1,024 `avx` (the first chunk) and 7,168 `avx+amx`.
- Live reads (9b3832eb4b, 2026-09-24): while runtron ran, a poller read `summary`, `<class>_totals` and `<class>_forwards` under `<worktree>/stats/instance-2/model/<id>/attention/` every 15 s. The switch-unset run showed `"on":false` and `{}` for the totals leaves. The switch-on run showed `"on":true` and rising counts (`fuse-poll.log`).
- Kill switch (`TRON_AMX_DISABLE=1` on the same binary with the switch set, prompt 1024, one run each, 9b3832eb4b, 2026-09-24). Decode, AMX on: 10,285,056 AMX visits and 0 AVX full-page visits. Decode, kill switch: 0 AMX visits and 10,285,056 AVX full-page visits. Prefill, AMX on: 16,515,072 AMX visits and 1,216,512 AVX full-page visits. Prefill, kill switch: 0 and 17,731,584. The identity `avx_full_page (kill) == amx + avx_full_page (on)` holds in both classes. The K tokens scored in software are equal in both arms (676,823,040 decode, 1,209,139,200 prefill). The counters see the same work whichever path served it.

## What the leaves look like

Read live during a switch-on run (this branch at bff317e0d3, delphi-3bda, 2026-09-29, dev-build mount `<worktree>/stats/instance-2/model/ingested-qwen-3-4b-instruct-2507-tp2/attention/`):

The samples above come from these runs: the stderr summary from the first, the worker leaves from the second.
