title: Drop a redundant const_cast from the signaled latch
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Remove the redundant `const_cast` from the signaled latch's readiness accessor to make its use of the mutable readiness word explicit. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

The latch declares `ready` as `mutable std::atomic_uint64_t`, so `&ready` already has the non-const pointer type required by `readiness_source::atomic`, even inside `readiness() const`. Pass that address directly; the cast performs no conversion and obscures why the access is valid.

title: Remove redundant token-position codegen test
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

Removes the `LoopyTronSpec` test "token_job_positions input keeps typed token-job index". It guards nothing that other tests don't already guard. There are no production code changes.

## Why it is redundant

The test checks that indexing a framework input in generated C++ renders as `outer_state.token_job_positions[ix]`, not with the loop counter's numeric value (`ix.i`). The code that could emit `ix.i` was removed in #3005, and index rendering does not depend on which input is indexed.

The test "slice codegen keeps typed batch row for sub-row slices" already covers the same path: it renders a function input as `outer_state.input[ix]` and rejects `ix.i` anywhere in the output.

The fixture `tokenPositionsModule` stays, because `ropeConfigModule` builds on it.

title: Keep the dense+MoE FFN from instantiating the single-kind runs
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

`feed_forward`'s `run` now chains its dense+MoE, dense-only and MoE-only cases with `else if constexpr`, so a model with both shared and routed experts no longer instantiates single-kind runs it never executes. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

## Why

At runtime the old and new code are identical, because the dense+MoE branch returned before reaching the other two. The difference is at compile time. The three cases were separate `if constexpr` statements, and a model where `has_dense && has_moe` holds also satisfies `has_dense` and `has_moe` on their own. So the compiler instantiated `dense.run(..., os_ffn_channel, ...)` and `moe.run(..., os_ffn_channel, ...)` even though the `return` kept them from running.

With `else if constexpr`, those branches are discarded and never instantiated. `run_main_help` already works this way.

Today the dead instantiation compiles, and no hand-written config has both kinds of experts. In `TRON_LLAMA_CONFIG`, the dense models are `1, 1, 0` and Mixtral is `8, 0, 2`. So nothing observable changes now.

The change isn't entirely superfluous, though. An upcoming PR checks at compile time that a matmul's output channel takes its readiness from the matmul's weights. In a dense+MoE model `os_ffn_channel` is host-written, because worker 0 fills it with the sum of the dense and MoE outputs. The dead `dense.run` instantiation, which writes W2 straight into `os_ffn_channel`, would fail that check. This PR removes that instantiation before the check arrives.

title: Correct the aliased-query and channel-backing descriptions
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Two channel descriptions are corrected: llama's prepare-order comment and the attention design doc now say that `qs`'s `prepare` writes NaN triggers into the queries that `qs_roped` aliases, and the tron-ingest skill names the channel's backing correctly.

## Aliased queries

`qs_roped` is a reference to `qs`: RoPE rewrites the raw WQ output in place. `qs_channel` uses a payload latch, `tensor_latch<wq_t>`. The device writes each item directly, and readiness is detected through NaN triggers in the item itself. At the start of each phase, the channel's `prepare` writes those triggers into every item (`fill_nans`).

So in `prepare_wq`, the first write into the shared buffer for a new layer is `qs_channel.prepare()`, not the WQ matmul. `qs_roped_channel.prepare()` runs first because it waits for the previous layer's attention readers to finish. That is what keeps attention from seeing the triggers.

The comment and the doc said only that readers must retire before WQ overwrites Q. That is true but incomplete. A reader could conclude that `qs`'s prepare is free to move earlier. If it did, attention could read NaN triggers in place of queries; this is an inferred risk, not an observed failure. Both texts now name the prepare as well as the matmul.

## Channel backing

The skill's plugin-anatomy reference described the backing as `latch_t::backing`, which doesn't exist. The channel's backing is `channel_backing<latch_t::scope, Ix, T, latch_t>`, specialized for whole-phase and per-item readiness.

title: Wait for MoE blend weights where a channel guards them
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Generated `moe_blend` kernels now wait for their blend weights whenever a channel guards that buffer, as they already do for the expert outputs they blend.

## Problem

`moeBlend` emits its kernel through `staticStrategy`. That helper's read-buffer list decides what each worker waits for. For every listed buffer that has a guard channel, it emits `start_reading_at` twice: once for the worker's first item before the traced loop, and once for each item inside it.

`moeBlend` passed an empty list, although its body reads `weights[tok]` for every token. The expert outputs it blends are waited on separately, one routed slot at a time. The weights were the only read with no wait.

Liveness analysis records that read as a parallel consumer (`Read (ParC QBatchItems)`). So the weights buffer gets a channel whenever it doesn't meet the no-channel rule: a parallel producer whose parallel consumers all share its iteration space (Note [No Channel for Par Kernels]). Examples are a producer in another domain, such as a matmul, or an extra consumer of another kind. In that case the kernel would read `weights[tok]` without waiting for it: a silent race, not a stall.

This is latent today. In every generated MoE plugin, the blend weights come from a kernel striped over the same items, so no channel exists. All 18 plugins regenerate byte-identically with this change.

## Change

Pass `blendWeightsBuf` as a read buffer. `staticStrategy` maps it to its guard channel and emits nothing when there isn't one, so today's plugins are unchanged. When a channel does appear, the weights get the same per-item wait as every other kernel input.

title: Give each consumer domain its own reset participant count
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

`generateResetCall` now gets each consumer domain's participant count from a per-domain function, `domainCount`, mainly so that the next PR's diff shows only how those counts are combined. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

## Change

The single-domain branch of the consumer count used to match `consumer` against the single-domain pattern synonyms. `MatrixC n`, for example, stands for `ConsumerDomains (MatrixConsumer n :| [])`. It now matches `consumerDomains consumer` against `domain NE.:| []` and hands that one domain to `domainCount :: ConsumerDomain k -> Expr`.

`domainCount` has one arm per `ConsumerDomain` constructor, each mapping one-to-one to an old arm (`MatrixC n` becomes `MatrixConsumer n`, `ParC _` becomes `ParConsumer _`, and so on), with the same counts and comments. The old fallback arm, `ConsumerDomains _ -> error …`, becomes `_ -> error …` on the domain list. The mixed branch, which adds the matrix count to `n_workers` when a consumer has a parallel domain, is unchanged.

With the counts in `domainCount`, #4644 can replace both branches with a sum over the consumer's domains, and its diff contains only that. All 18 generated plugins regenerate byte-identically.

title: Merge the two single-host channel consumer kinds
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Merge the two single-host channel consumer kinds so MoE routing and attention K/V submission share one participation contract, with readiness determined by the producer.

## Why the distinction is unnecessary

`SingleHostConsumer` and `PerItemSingleHostConsumer` both describe one main-thread reader with main-thread-only synchronization. Their difference was readiness: C++ generation forced `SingleHostConsumer` channels to use `fallback_producer_t`, which waits for every producer to finish the phase, while the per-item variant retained the producer's latch.

MoE routing used the whole-phase variant for its top-k expert indices. Those indices are written by parallel host kernels that already publish each token's output with `finish_writing_at`, and routing already calls `start_reading_at` for every token before reading the indices. The consumer therefore has the item-level synchronization it needs without forcing a whole-phase latch.

## One single-host contract

Keep `SingleHostConsumer` and remove its per-item counterpart. C++ generation now retains the producer-selected latch for this consumer: host-produced MoE indices use `signaled_producer_t`, as host-produced attention K/V already did. Synchronization still runs only on the main thread, and these channels still count all producer workers and one consumer.

For example, if a helper has published the indices for a token but has not finished its producer phase, routing can now complete that token's readiness wait. The routing builder still runs only after the existing loop has waited for every token's indices; this does not make routing construction incremental.

Attention K/V accesses and their checker now use the surviving kind. It also inherits the restriction against direct function inputs: both MoE routing and attention K/V submission require an explicit channel, which an unchannelled input cannot provide.

## Validation

Updated lowering/code-generation tests check that host-produced K/V and MoE indices retain per-item latches and one-consumer reset counts. The MoE scheduling case continues to check the producer-to-routing synchronization order. Input validation now checks that the unified single-host kind rejects an unchannelled function input.

title: ci: Keep an interrupted runtime copy removable
author: jadams-positron
body:
## Summary

Test and benchmark runtime preparation copied `gen/` out of the Nix store with `shutil.copytree`, which keeps the store's `0555` directory modes, and made the directories writable only afterwards. A job cancelled in between left read-only directories in the runner workspace. After that, every job on that runner failed in `actions/checkout` with `EACCES` until someone cleaned the workspace by hand. That happened to `andoria-14-0` on 2026-09-26.

`runtime_staging.copy_runtime_tree` replaces `copytree` plus `make_directories_writable` in both callers. It creates each directory with the source mode plus owner-write before copying into it, so a partial tree is always removable. Files and symlinks are still copied with `copy2` (symlinks as links). Once a directory's children are copied, it gets the source's atime and mtime back at nanosecond precision, still owner-writable.

One deliberate difference from `copytree`: the copy stops at the first error instead of collecting errors and raising at the end. Either way, `prepare` fails.

## How to Review

1. `bin/ci/tron-build/runtime_staging.py`: `copy_runtime_tree`. The invariant is that no destination directory is ever without `S_IWUSR`. Timestamps are restored last because copying children changes them.
2. `bin/ci/tron-build/test_runtime.py` and `benchmark_runtime.py`: one-line call-site swaps; `shutil` is no longer imported.
3. `bin/ci/tron-build/test_test_runtime.py`:
   - `test_interrupted_prepare_leaves_gen_removable` forks a child that prepares a read-only store tree. The child pauses at a pipe rendezvous right after the nested directory is copied, and the parent then SIGKILLs it, with bounded waits. The test checks that the partial tree is owner-writable and that plain `shutil.rmtree` removes the workspace. The `copystat` hook makes the old `copytree` implementation pause at the same point, after it has set the nested directory back to `0555`.
   - The materialization test now also asserts that copied directory timestamps match the source.
   - `_make_stores` is the existing test's store fixture, moved out so both tests share it.

## Testing

- The SIGKILL test run against the old `copytree` implementation fails, with `PermissionError` removing `gen/src/tron`. On this branch, `python3 -m unittest -v test_test_runtime` passes all 7 tests (macOS, Python 3.14).
- PR CI at `b7f923abc3`: every check passed. That includes CI machinery contracts, Lint, and Test host and Test FPGA on DUT runners, which ran "Restore exact Nix test runtime" through the new copy. Benchmarks were skipped by label.
- `nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.ci-machinery-contracts -L` at `8d26f28088`, before the timestamp and SIGKILL follow-up, on an x86_64 Linux host: passes.
- `uvx ruff@0.15.1 format --check` and `ruff check` on the changed files: clean.

Closes #4655

title: Reject per-item publication on payload-published channels
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Reject explicit per-item publication on channels whose payload signals readiness, catching incompatible host-producer wiring at compile time and removing ineffective publication calls from matmul callbacks.

## Make publication match the producer

Block latches, including those used by `dtensor` and result-partitioned `ptensor` matmuls, detect readiness by watching the final bytes of each payload block or tile. Their `finish_writing` methods were no-ops, but their presence allowed `channel::finish_writing_at` to compile. The channel documentation also required those calls, and handwritten matmul callbacks looped over completed items solely to invoke them.

That interface could hide an incompatible producer choice. Ordinary CPU kernels need explicit publication because their tensor stores do not guarantee the ordering required by payload-based readiness. Selecting a block latch for such a kernel still compiled, even when its `finish_writing_at` call provided no synchronization. The earlier native LLaMA fix in `419f362fb4` changed host-produced channels to `signaled_producer_t`; this PR makes publication calls reject that old wiring.

## Enforce the distinction at the channel boundary

Remove the no-op methods from payload-based latches and constrain both `finish_writing_at` overloads to channels whose backing supports the operation. Signaled channels retain the call that publishes an item through a separate readiness word. Whole-phase fallback channels also retain the call as a no-op, allowing host kernels to report item completion while consumers wait for every producer's phase completion.

Dense FFN, MoE, and LLaMA matmul callbacks drop their per-item publication loops, including the MoE routed-slot helper. They retain `finish_writing` and input-release callbacks: payload readiness does not replace the phase barrier that protects buffer reuse. The channel and latch notes now distinguish host-kernel item publication from matmul completion.

## Validation

The existing block-channel test replaces its runtime check that `finish_writing_at` has no effect with a compile-time assertion that the typed-index call is unavailable. It retains the checks that payload writes make individual items ready and that preparing the next phase clears readiness.

title: Require nonempty payloads in tensor latch bind
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Tensor latches that use a payload's own last 8 bytes as their readiness signal now reject zero-length tensors at compile time, instead of pointing that signal outside the buffer.

## Problem

Two `tensor_latch` specializations, `tensor_latch<block_producer_t>` and the ptensor one, have no separate readiness word. Each uses the last 8 bytes of the payload instead:

1. `bind()` computes `trigger = reinterpret_cast<volatile uint64_t*>(end) - 1`.
2. `fill_nans()` sets those bytes to an all-ones NaN marker.
3. The consumer waits, via `mwaitx`, for the producer to overwrite them.

The only size check on `bind()` and `fill_nans()` is that the payload's byte size is a multiple of 8, and a zero-length tensor passes it (`0 % 8 == 0`). For such a tensor, `tensor_latch<block_producer_t>::bind` sets `end == begin`, so `trigger` points 8 bytes before the payload. `fill_nans()` then writes the marker there, out of bounds, and `wait()` watches memory that doesn't belong to the tensor. This risk comes from reading the code: no current instantiation latches a zero-length tensor.

## Approach

`Tensor::size_ > 0` is added to the `requires` clauses of `bind()` and `fill_nans()` in both specializations. Binding a zero-length payload now fails the constraint at the call site, in the per-item channel backing, instead of compiling into an out-of-bounds write. Existing instantiations all have nonzero size, so none of them changes. The check is compile-time only, with no runtime cost.

In the ptensor specialization, a zero-length result (`M == 0`) produces zero tiles and so no triggers, so the loops never compute `end - 1`. The constraint is added there only so both specializations accept the same payloads.

title: Make MoE per-token routing and batch ranks private
author: mitchelldalvirosen-positron
body:
## Summary

Make `moe_routing`'s per-token routing pointer and batch-rank table private, so callers read them only through the existing `per_token()` and `batch_rank()` accessors. This is a behavior-preserving refactor.

`reset()` builds the batch-rank table from `batch_tokens`: each batch token maps to its position in the batch, and every other token maps to `invalid_batch_rank()`, so `batch_rank()` asserts for a token outside the current batch. The table was public and writable, so a caller could change an entry without changing `batch_tokens`; `batch_rank()` would then return the wrong rank instead of asserting. The per-token routing pointer was also public, although its comment already directed access through `per_token()`.

Neither member is accessed outside `moe_routing`. Both move below `private:`, next to the row storage that #4493 made private, and are renamed `per_token_` and `batch_rank_by_token_` to match the other private members. Call sites do not change.

`batch_tokens` stays public. Matmul readiness remapping reads `routing.batch_tokens.size()` to size its remapped waitables, so hiding it would need a new accessor and call-site changes.

title: Plan experts with uniform loads when no load profile exists
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

With no expert-load profile, tensor-parallel MoE plugins place expert weights by visit-order rotation: each tile goes to the next card in the order the plugin visits tensors. Generated plugins visit each expert weight in its own loop over experts, so all of an expert's weights usually land on one card. Where gate and up are separate weights (Qwen3), that card runs the two independent matmuls one after the other.

Load-aware placement already avoids this when a profile exists. It plans each expert onto a card and puts tensor ID t (gate 0, up 1, down 2) t cards past it. This PR uses that plan with uniform loads when there is no profile, for tensor-parallel plugins whose expert weights are one tile each: the generated plugins. Handwritten Mixtral 8x7B and 8x22B, single-card runs and plugins with a profile keep today's placement.

Measured against main, GPT-OSS 20B on 2 and 4 cards is faster on every measure (time to first token 4.6–5.7% shorter, decode 4.0–5.9% faster). Qwen3-30B-A3B on 4 cards decodes 5.6% faster. This gives the same results as #4671 (closed), which added a separate placement strategy, and it lets #4367 move Qwen3 to the CPU router.

## Changes

1. **Uniform plan by default** (`h/tron/models/model.hpp`, [Note [Expert placement without a load profile]](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/blob/9c3dc4725f6c9c6b7fe5aa399a1f015a50ed2743/h/tron/models/model.hpp#L965)). With no profile and no replicas requested, `maybe_wrap_experts_by_load` plans with `expert_load_profile_t::uniform` if the model is tensor-parallel and every expert weight is one tile. The uniform profile steers placement only; `--expert-routing load` needs a measured profile.
2. **One-tile check** (`h/tron/models/model.hpp`, `h/tron/hardware/ptensor.hpp`, `h/tron/hardware/permuted.hpp`, `src/tron/hardware/placer.cpp`). The plan gives every tile of an expert weight the same cards, which would collapse a tiled weight onto one card. Loading visits the plugin's expert weights once and counts their tiles with a new `hardware::tile_count`, which also looks through `permuted_tensor`. Generated plugins qualify: their expert weights are `expert_dtensor_t`, which is TP1 by design. Handwritten Mixtral does not: its w2 is tiled at tp2, and all three weights at tp4. If a tiled weight still reaches a no-profile plan, `ExpertsByPlan` aborts on its second tile.
3. **Logs and docs** (`config.hpp`, `placer.hpp`, `expert_placement_plan.cpp`, `src/rinzler.cpp`, `bin/expert_distribution.py`): one log line per placement decision, and the docs point to the new Note.
4. **Tests** (`t/t_placer.cpp`, `t/t_expert_placement.cpp`): a generated-style test plugin on 2 and 4 cards gets the plan; handwritten Mixtral tp2 and tp4 (plain and permuted visits), one card, and load-aware placement off keep the base placement; the abort fires on a tiled expert weight.

## Throughput

Main (`1feddd0dcd`) against main with this change, both linking the same plugins, with no profile. Each user sends a 2,048-token prompt and generates 512 tokens. Each entry is the median of six paired `runtron` runs; "(noise)" marks entries where the pairs did not all agree or the change was below the noise threshold.

| Model | Cards | Users | Time to first token | Decode speed per user | Total output rate |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| GPT-OSS 20B | 2 | 1 | 4.6% shorter | 5.9% faster | 5.6% higher |
| GPT-OSS 20B | 4 | 1 | 4.9% shorter | 4.0% faster | 4.3% higher |
| GPT-OSS 20B | 4 | 4 | 5.7% shorter | 5.5% faster | 5.8% higher |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 4 | 4 | 0.1% shorter (noise) | 5.6% faster | 3.4% higher |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 2 | 4 | 0.2% longer (noise) | no change (noise) | 0.1% lower (noise) |

- Against #4671 in the same session, all five configurations tie on every measure.
- With #4367's CPU router and this change, Qwen3 on 4 cards is faster than with the FPGA router: time to first token 12.6% shorter, decode 2.1% faster, total output 6.8% higher.
- These builds apply the change to `1feddd0dcd`. At this PR's head, placement is identical to the measured builds for every plugin above.

## Not in this PR

- **Tiled expert weights under a plan.** With a measured profile or `--num-expert-replicas`, handwritten Mixtral's tiled expert weights are still planned onto one card each, as on main.
- **Generated Mixtral 8x7B** takes the plan but was not timed. Its layout was checked on hardware.

## Testing

- Hardware placement logs for 13 model and card-count combinations match the expected maps tensor for tensor. Generated plugins match the uniform plan; handwritten Mixtral 8x7B, 8x22B and GPT-OSS 120B match main.
- Removing the one-tile check or the `permuted_tensor` tile count makes `t_placer` fail, and disabling the abort makes `t_expert_placement` fail. A build without the `permuted_tensor` tile count aborts while loading permuted Mixtral on hardware.

title: feat(rinzler): accept reasoning_effort xhigh; processors reject unrenderable literals at encode
author: positron-mark
body:
Accept `"xhigh"` as a valid `reasoning_effort` literal. Whether a literal can be
honored is decided by the selected token processor at prompt preparation, not by
the controller. Request-side kwargs/effort extraction moves into a shared helper
(`extract_chat_template_request_fields`) used by both `chat_completion_request::from_json`
and the Drogon-free host tests.

## Principle

- `VALID_REASONING_EFFORTS` is the request vocabulary: what parses.
  `validate_chat_template_kwargs` checks vocabulary and value types for known
  keys, never cross-model capability.
- A processor decides at `encode_conversation` what it can honor and throws for
  what it cannot. Harmony: `low|medium|high` (rejects `none` and `xhigh`). HF:
  whatever the template reads — ATEM maps effort to `reasoning_strength`, which
  accepts `xhigh`; Gemma 4 maps `none` to `enable_thinking=false` and everything
  else to `true`; legacy templates see the string. Native Qwen (#4709): 3.8's
  template validates effort itself; 3.6's ignores it, and the adapter rejects
  `xhigh` there explicitly.
- Server defaults (`RZ_CHAT_TEMPLATE_KWARGS`) get the same vocabulary/type
  validation as requests and nothing more. A server-default literal a model
  cannot honor is a per-request 400 naming the literal — the contract
  `reasoning_effort="none"` already has on Harmony.

## Behavior changes vs `main`

- `xhigh` is accepted by any processor whose template can honor it: ATEM/Glimmer
  (`reasoning_strength: xhigh`), legacy HF templates (string passes through), and
  Gemma 4 (`enable_thinking=true`). On `main` every path returned 400.
- A top-level `xhigh` on Harmony changes from `Invalid JSON in request body`
  (parse-time literal rejection) to
  `Failed to encode prompt: Harmony does not support reasoning_effort='xhigh'`
  (text/plain HTTP 400 unchanged).
- A server-default `xhigh` does not exit at startup; on a Harmony model it is a
  per-request 400 — identical in kind to a server-default `none` on `main`.
- Literal-validation errors list the accepted values from `VALID_REASONING_EFFORTS`
  (now including `xhigh`) instead of a hardcoded list. An invalid top-level literal
  is still a client-facing `Invalid JSON in request body` 400; the detailed message
  only appears in the server log.

## Tests

- `t_rinzler_request`: a JSON `null` top-level `reasoning_effort` is treated as
  unset and keeps the server default; Gemma 4 `xhigh` → `enable_thinking=true`.

title: Reduce tool calling grammar complexity for gemma4 and glimmer
author: positron-mark
body:
This PR changes how the gemma4 and glimmer (ATEM) tool-call grammars stop the model from writing forbidden text inside free-form string values. Gemma 4 forbids its string delimiter, its tool-call close marker and any request stop text. Glimmer forbids the two enclosing close tags and any request stop text. Previously, each forbidden text got its own exclusion terminal, and each was added to the string lexeme as a separate negated conjunct. llguidance's lexer cost grows with the number of those conjuncts: with enough stop texts it ran out of lexer fuel, and on a qwen3.x tokenizer (in another branch) six conjuncts failed grammar construction outright.

Both gemma4 and glimmer grammars now build one alternation terminal that matches any string containing any forbidden text, and negate it once. The accepted language is the same, but the lexer sees one exclusion no matter how many stop texts a request carries. Duplicate and empty stop texts are dropped before the terminal is built, and a single shared helper builds and regex-escapes it for both grammars. Two small hardening changes come along: warnings about client-supplied stop texts now log a bounded, escaped prefix instead of the raw text, and a compile-time check enforces that the two fixed Gemma 4 markers a payload can contain — the string delimiter and the tool-call close marker — contain <, which the '<'-free key and bare-value charsets rely on to exclude them.

title: Raise the reasoning request's max_tokens to 1024
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

After #4367, GPT-OSS-20B uses the CPU MoE router and answers `REASONING_CHAT_REQUEST` ("What is 17 * 23? Think it through step by step, then give the final answer.") in 354–371 completion tokens, against 151–277 with the FPGA router. With `max_tokens` 400 that leaves at most 46 tokens of headroom, and rinzler's output varies from request to request, so the GPT-OSS reasoning rows in `t_rinzler-slow` sometimes hit the limit:

- "Reasoning present" failed #4367's first merge-queue run (GCP Nix run 36645451626).
- "Oversized reasoning budget is inert", which requires the answer to stop on its own, failed 3 of 16 local runs.

This PR raises the request's `max_tokens` to 1024. Every observed answer stops by 365 tokens.

## Changes

- `REASONING_CHAT_REQUEST`: `max_tokens` 400 → 1024.
- The two Gemma-4-12B "Reasoning present by default" rows drop their `max_tokens = 768` override, which existed only to get above 400. They now use the request's 1024.
- Comments that named 400 now name 1024. The reasoning-budget rows keep their own 1536.

title: Move GPT-OSS-120B to the CPU router
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

GPT-OSS-120B switches to the CPU MoE router (`ingest.moe_router: cpu`), as GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3-30B-A3B did in #4367. The FPGA router multiplies with INT4 weights and picks a different top-4 expert set from the checkpoint's own router in 28% of token-layers; the CPU router differs in 2.9%, only at BF16 near-ties. With 4 and 8 users on 4 cards, time to first token is 2.5–2.9% shorter. With one user, decode is 0.9–1.2% slower.

## Changes

- `config/models.yaml`: `moe_router: cpu` for `ingested_gpt_oss_120b`.
- `config/test_model_definitions.py`: the router-policy tests pin 120B to `cpu`, and use Mixtral 8x7B as their real `fpga`-registered model, which 120B used to be.
- `ingest/README.md`: lists 120B among the `cpu` models.

## Accuracy

Four 2,048-token prompts on the same two cards. Each router is compared with the checkpoint's router computed exactly on that run's own inputs, over 303,876 token-layers.

| Router | Top-4 expert set differs | Top-1 expert differs |
|---|---|---|
| FPGA (INT4 weights) | 27.99% | 7.96% |
| CPU (BF16) | 2.94% | 0.87% |

Every CPU-router miss is a near-tie within 2 BF16 steps. There is no end-to-end logit test for 120B.

## Throughput

FPGA router against CPU router in one binary, with identical expert placement (120B ships a measured load profile). Each user sends a 2,048-token prompt and generates 512 tokens. Each entry is the median of six paired `runtron` runs; "(noise)" marks entries where the pairs did not all agree or the change was below the noise threshold.

| Cards | Users | Time to first token | Decode speed per user | Total output rate |
|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1 | 1.0% shorter | 1.2% slower | 0.5% lower |
| 4 | 1 | 0.3% longer (noise) | 0.9% slower | 0.8% lower |
| 4 | 4 | 2.5% shorter | no change (noise) | 1.1% higher (noise) |
| 4 | 8 | 2.9% shorter | 0.8% faster (noise) | 1.9% higher |

- The single-user decode loss appears in all six pairs at both card counts, about 30–70 µs per token.
- Not measured: 2 cards with several users, and CI's two-instance setup.

## Not in this PR

- Keeping the router's logits in FP32. In an offline replay of the CPU router on the same inputs it removes all remaining misses; #4366's round-to-nearest stores do not. That is a separate PR.
- The `tp1` and `host` executors listed for 120B. It does not fit on one card with either router (HBM allocation fails during load), and the host executor needs about 460 GB for FP32 expert weights.

## Testing

- The 120B plugin built from the registry is identical to the one measured above, apart from trace-id comments.
- Setting 120B or Mixtral 8x7B to the other router makes the router-policy tests fail.

title: Remove AVX-512 build guard and always compile with explicit AVX-512 flags
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

Every machine we build for supports AVX-512, and no real build turns the `AVX512` CMake option off. The only way to get `AVX512=OFF` was the `BUILD_NATIVE` lscpu probe on a host without AVX-512, and on main that configuration does not compile (`h/tron/simd/fp32.hpp` uses `fp32x16` outside any guard). This PR removes the option and everything that served the off state: the `TRON_AVX512_ENABLED` define and its branches, the 8-wide chunk-size code, the host probe, and the preset that only toggled AVX-512.

## Changes

**CMake**

1. Remove `option(AVX512)`, `option(BUILD_NATIVE)` and the lscpu probe.
2. `tron`, `pos`, `librinzler` and `tron_model_compile_config` always get the AVX-512 flag set. `TRON_AVX512_ENABLED` is gone.

**C++**

3. Remove every `#if`/`#ifdef TRON_AVX512_ENABLED` and keep the AVX-512 branch (`simd/`, kernels, tensor, `mask.hpp`, three tests).
4. Second commit: remove every `TRON_CHUNK_SIZE == 8` / `!= 16` branch, including the contiguous V layout in the KV cache, the AVX2 `scaled_v_expr` and the five `if constexpr (chunk_size == 8)` branches in `expr.hpp`. `TRON_CHUNK_SIZE` stays defined as 16.
5. `mask.hpp` guards `mask_t<512>` with `__AVX512VPOPCNTDQ__`, because `pos_fake` translation units include it without the AVX-512 flags.

**Presets, GNUmakefile, Nix**

6. Remove the `cross-avx512` preset. `darwin` and `deb` drop their `BUILD_NATIVE`/`AVX512` settings.
7. GNUmakefile picks `native` on every Linux host. The `HAS_AVX512` run guards and the "executable will not run on this machine" warning stay. The REMOTE special case for `gen/.preset_stamp` goes, since submitter and worker now pick the same preset.
8. `flake.nix` and `nix/cmake-tron-test-build.nix` drop `-DBUILD_NATIVE=OFF -DAVX512=ON`.

**Docs**

9. Rewrite Note [Cross-Compile for AVX-512] in `GNUmakefile` and the preset paragraph in `README.ci.md`, and fix the V layout quoted in `doc/token_tree_v2.md`.

## Behaviour changes

- The `cross-avx512` preset is gone. A `gen/` stamped with it reconfigures once as `native`.
- `-DAVX512` and `-DBUILD_NATIVE` are no longer project options; passing them has no effect.
- Configure no longer runs `lscpu`. On a host without AVX-512, `native`, `asan`, `tsan` and `coverage` now cross-compile for AVX-512 instead of producing an `AVX512=OFF` tree that fails to compile. `make t_*` and the Slice test targets still refuse to run there. `test-tsan`, `test-asan` and the coverage targets have no such guard: they build, then die with SIGILL.
- The `darwin` preset compiles with the AVX-512 flag set. The macOS C++ build does not link today either way.
- With `REMOTE=1`, the submitting host rewrites a stale `gen/.preset_stamp` instead of leaving it for the worker.

## Testing

- `make build-test` and the host test suite, `[slow]` cases included, pass on an AVX-512 host. FPGA tests are left to CI.
- In the native, deb, nix, asan, tsan and coverage configurations, every compile command matches main except for the dropped `-DTRON_AVX512_ENABLED`.
- The preprocessed output of all 2,443 translation-unit builds in those configurations matches main token for token, apart from `__LINE__` values and the removed `if constexpr (chunk_size == 8)` branches in `expr.hpp`, which were never instantiated.

title: Pin the re-promoted Qwen3.5 27B GPTQ checkpoint
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

This PR moves CI's pin for the Qwen3.5 27B GPTQ checkpoint, `positron-ai/Qwen_Qwen3.5-27B-ingest-best-gptq`, from the revision that publishes its 2026-06-30 promotion to the one that publishes its 2026-09-29 promotion. On andoria, the local checkpoint name `positron-ai/Qwen--Qwen3.5-27B-ingest-best-gptq` already points at the new promotion; CI stages the pinned revision under that same name.

The new promotion was re-quantized with gptqmodel 7.5.0 (the earlier one used 7.1.0) and keeps the same tensor names, shapes and shard layout. Its `config.json` declares `model_type: qwen3_5_text`, the type Transformers uses for the Qwen3.5 text model; the old file declared the wrapper type `qwen3_5`. That lets the checkpoint be its own configuration source. A Qwen3.5 27B registration, to be posted on top of #3696, relies on this: #3696's configuration reader accepts a `qwen3_5` config.json only with the published 4B geometry, so it rejects the old 27B file, and it reads a `qwen3_5_text` file directly.

## Background

- **Pin.** A `ModelSpec` in `bin/ci/prime_hf_models.py`: a Hugging Face repository at an exact revision, its file list, and the name CI stages it under. This pin is structural: its file list names the weight shards, but CI stages only the other files (configuration, tokenizer, chat templates, shard index and quantization metadata). The re-quantized weights therefore do not reach CI; CI sees the new `config.json` and quantization metadata.
- **Promotion.** A dated checkpoint directory on andoria, `_promoted/<name>--<date>`. The undated local name points at the current one.
- **Configuration source.** What a registry entry's `ingest.hf_id` names. Export reads `config.json` and the tokenizer from it.

## Changes

1. **Pin.** The revision moves to the one that publishes the 2026-09-29 promotion. The file list, destination and snapshot kind are unchanged, and the new revision contains every listed file.
2. **Tests.** `bin/ci/test_prime_hf_models.py` expects the new revision.

## Testing

title: Record Perfetto kernel events in a private tracefs instance
author: bretcraig-positron
body:
Tron's Perfetto kernel captures now record into a private tracefs instance, `instances/tron`, so they no longer reset the top-level instance that other tools share.

## Problem
A `linux.ftrace` source without `instance_name` makes Perfetto take over the top-level tracefs instance, `/sys/kernel/tracing`. At setup it turns every event off and clears and resizes the buffer; at teardown it shrinks the buffer to one page per CPU. Any other recorder there, such as `nfs-delegation-recorder`, silently stops recording.

## Solution
The checked-in kernel configs now record into `instances/tron`, and the wrapper's default config comments out its ftrace source, which selected no events but still reset the top-level instance. `perfetto/generate-config` rejects a `linux.ftrace` source that lacks a valid `instance_name` or uses a setting named instances don't support (atrace, `enable_function_graph`, `kprobe_events`). `perfetto/launcher-common` creates each missing instance before the daemons start and removes only the instances its run created; when it can't create or write one, it runs `sudo chown` on `instances/` and that instance.

## Testing
`perfetto-config-check` (`perfetto/test_perfetto.py`, 58 tests against a fake tracefs) and the CI Lint script (`bin/ci/run-lint-checks.sh`) pass at this head.
With another recorder using the top-level tracefs instance, two `nix run .#wrapper -- -c rinzler --os-events -w` captures, one run for its full 10 s and one stopped with SIGINT, recorded scheduling, syscall, and interrupt events through `instances/tron`. The top-level instance's settings stayed unchanged, and each capture removed the instance on exit.

title: Keep token input array semantics uniform in Loopy
author: bgamari-positron
body:
Previously, indexing a width-one array produced a scalar for framework inputs (e.g. `token_job_tokens` and `token_job_positions`) but a row for intermediate buffers. Loopy checking and lowering depended on where the variable was bound.

Loopy now requires explicit element indexing for both kinds of array. `LoopyTron` preserves their row shape. `TronCpp` adapts framework token and position storage with read-only row views and copies rows with `strided_copy`.

Addresses the layering violation identified in https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/3267.

title: Require a scalar RoPE position in Loopy
author: rbjarnason-positron
body:
## Summary

LoopyCheck now rejects a RoPE token position that is a whole row rather than an integer scalar. This follows #4747.

## Background

Since #4747, framework inputs such as `token_job_positions` are width-one rows in Loopy, so `token_job_positions[ix][0]` is the element. LoopyCheck still accepted any integer row as the RoPE position, so `token_job_positions[ix]` passed. TronCpp renders that row as a read-only row view, and an intermediate row as a tensor. `tron::rope` takes a `uint32_t` position and neither type converts to it, so the generated C++ would not compile. BulkLoopy already emits the element read, so real models are unaffected.

## Changes

- Check the RoPE position as an integer scalar, and name it in the singular in the diagnostic.
- Use the element form for framework-input reads in the kernel access fixtures: the RoPE positions, and the per-layer embedding fixture's lookup index.
- Add a LoopyCheck case that rejects a whole-row position.

title: Retire matmul callbacks before a minibatch is destroyed
author: jw-pos
body:
A matmul's completion callback can still be queued or running when `forward()` destroys the minibatch it touches. This PR makes the batch wait for every matmul callback before any of its members, or the latch arena behind them, is destroyed. It fixes a latent race on main. It was found in review of #4504, which carried a different fix.

## Problem

A device matmul's completion callback runs on an RX thread and finishes the minibatch's channels. Nothing on the forward pass waits for it:

- the matmul's consumers read its result through the payload, so the callback is on no consumer's path;
- the last phase of a channel has no next `prepare()` that would wait on its producers.

`forward()` can therefore return, and destroy the batch and clear the arena (`q_batches.clear()`), while a callback is still queued or running. The callback then touches freed memory.

## Why reordering cannot fix it

The first idea was to reorder the callback so that `finishWriting(out)` is its last touch of the batch. That does not help. Whichever statement comes last still touches the batch after the point where nothing waits for it. The callback's lifetime has to be tied to the batch's lifetime.

## Fix

- The outer `batch` (`common.hpp`) owns a "matrix callbacks" latch, taken from the batch's latch arena, so `TRON_LATCH_WATCHDOG` reports outstanding callbacks.
- Every launch site increments the latch before it launches. A callback that runs synchronously, such as an MoE launch with no active experts, is therefore still counted.
- Each callback copies the `latch_ref` and counts down as its last statement.
- `~batch()` waits for the count to reach zero, before any member is destroyed and before `forward()` clears the arena.
- There is no `std::terminate`. `forward()` is `noexcept`, so an exception from a launch terminates there and never unwinds through the destructor. There is no wait in `reset_channels`.

Coverage:

- Translation (`TronCpp.hs`) emits the count and count-down at both the dense and the MoE launch of every generated plugin.
- The hand-written Llama plugin does the same for the `wq`, `wk`, `wv` and `wo` launches and the dense and MoE feed-forward launches. Its `plugin_batch` holds a copy of the outer latch.
- Note [Matrix callback lifetime] in `common.hpp` states the contract. Note [Plugin-owned worker launch], the TronCpp header and the TronCheck final-window comment now say that the batch, not `run()`, retires matmul callbacks.

## Cost

The cost was measured with paired ABAB runs on one andoria-08 card: ingested-llama-3.1-8b TP1, 128 tokens, 20 measured waves per variant, main against main + this PR. The figures are per-request decode tok/s medians.

| Users | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 129.3 | 130.5 |
| 4 | 89.4 | 89.1 |
| 4, aggregate | 249.4 | 248.6 |

The A/A spread is 0.3–0.6%, and both differences are well inside one standard deviation (2.4 tok/s at 1 user). GPT-OSS-120B TP4 was not measured.

These figures were measured on main 077e55f617. Later restacks onto newer main left the fix unchanged.

## Testing

- New `t_generate_host` case, "A generated plugin's matmul callbacks finish before forward() returns" (`[matrix-callbacks]`). It runs the generated ingested-llama-3.1-8b plugin under a test executor whose launches return at once and compute on a test-owned device thread. Each item's last 8 bytes are published last, and each callback arrives 200 ms later on a separate RX thread. Neither the host executor nor `pos_fake` can show the race, because both call back inline. The case runs one prefill pass that requests no logits. That leaves the last layer's callbacks outstanding when `forward()` returns. (With logits, the logits matmul's own delayed callback is queued after every layer's, which hides the race.)
  - **On main it fails:** `CHECK( invoked == launched )` with `218 == 224`.
  - **With the fix it passes**, 20 runs in a row. After the restack onto the current main it still passes.
  - It loads no checkpoint, so the weights stay zero pages. It takes 14–26 s and peaks at about 2.5 GB.
- The case is gated on the selected ingested-llama-3.1-8b plugin through `OPTIONAL_MODEL_REQUIREMENTS`. `t_generate_host` is labelled `fake`, so the required `Test host` job runs it. The CI test build sets `TRON_REQUIRE_ALL_MODEL_TESTS=ON`, so the case is always compiled there. It is also added to `make build-tsan`/`test-tsan`, filtered to `[matrix-callbacks]`.
- The whole of `t_generate_host` passes (3 cases, 2,931 assertions). The ingest tests pass. The FPGA golden case "Generate from a canned prompt with LLaMa 3.1 8B GPTQ from the ingest pipeline" passes on one card. lint-notes and the lint-toolchain check pass.
- Not covered by a test:
  - **The hand-written Llama plugin.** A llama-3-8b-host version of the case passes on main, because `~plugin_batch` already waits on the `os_ffn` producer barrier. It is therefore not added. The fix still covers Llama.
  - **MoE.** The GPT-OSS-20B plugin does not compile under the FP32 test executor; that would need a BF16 version of the executor.

title: Add --pay-for-determinism to rinzler
author: jw-pos
body:
rinzler gains `--pay-for-determinism`, the flag runtron already has. With it, two rinzler servers, or two runs of one, can be compared logprob for logprob. The default is unchanged.

## Problem

runtron's `--pay-for-determinism` (Note [Paying for Determinism]) fixes the attention worker split and turns off speed-based work autotuning, so that a model's logits depend only on its inputs. rinzler hard-codes `pay_for_determinism = false` when it builds the `model_config`. So even two single-host rinzler runs of the same requests can differ in the low bits of some logprobs, and serving output cannot be checked byte for byte against a reference. #4504's multi-host correctness runs need exactly that comparison.

## Changes

All in `src/rinzler.cpp`:

- a `pay_for_determinism` global, with a comment citing Note [Paying for Determinism];
- the load-time `model_config` takes `.pay_for_determinism = pay_for_determinism` instead of `false`;
- `--pay-for-determinism` is parsed, and logs "Paying for determinism";
- the help text:

  ```
    --pay-for-determinism  Make results reproducible: fixes the
                       attention worker split and disables
                       speed-based work autotuning, at a cost of
                       throughput (Note [Paying for Determinism])
  ```

## Cost

The cost was measured on one andoria-08 card (`--instance 7,8`): ingested-llama-3.1-8b-permuted TP1, `--max-batches 1 --max-concurrency 16`, and a fresh rinzler per run, alternating flag off and on. The load was streaming `/v1/completions` with a distinct ~400-token prompt per request and 128 output tokens (`ignore_eos`). Figures are aggregate output tok/s.

| Attention | Users | Off | On | Runs (off / on) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| hardware (default) | 1 | 85.2 | 85.1 | 4 / 3 |
| hardware (default) | 4 | 153.3 | 152.0 | 3 / 4 |
| software (`USE_HW_ATTN=0`) | 1 | 89.6 | 90.1 | 3 / 3 |
| software (`USE_HW_ATTN=0`) | 4 | 150.2 | 154.1 | 3 / 3 |

Each figure is the median of the clean runs. The host was shared (load average 27–62). Runs that other jobs slowed in both arms are excluded: the first hardware-attention round (about 15 tok/s in both arms), one off run at 4 users (54 tok/s) and one on run at 1 user (31 tok/s). With all runs, the hardware-attention medians are 84.2 / 83.7 at 1 user and 149.7 / 150.5 at 4 users. p50 inter-token latency was 7.4–8.2 ms at 1 user and 12.4–13.6 ms at 4 users, in both arms.

The difference is within run-to-run noise in this setup. With one minibatch the main/attention split is already fixed, so the flag only removes worker-speed weighting. Several minibatches or a larger model may cost more; that was not measured.

## Testing

- No new test: the change wires an existing `model_config` field, whose effect runtron already exercises.
- rinzler builds, `--help` shows the text above, and every flag-on run logs "Paying for determinism".
- `make lint-notes` and the lint-toolchain check pass. The help text keeps the Note's name on one line, so lint-notes resolves it.
- Used by #4504's validation: with this flag and `USE_HW_ATTN=0`, a three-host Atlas pipeline returned 12/12 responses identical to single-host rinzler, as did a two-process pipeline on andoria-08.
